## 1.08 The balance beam: the atom, physically


The atom has a physical archetype, and it is older than written number: the equal-arm balance. Load the two registers as the two pans and the correspondence is not analogy but anatomy — every structural fact of the atom is a working part of the beam, and the beam supplies the one thing a formal presentation cannot: the demonstration that the read costs nothing. (The correspondence runs far past this section: the Appendix — *The Pulse and the Beam: plain-words keys to the corpus* — retells the entire framework in plain words, its beam key twelve facts about this one instrument with a term-by-term key; the beam key is the recommended first read, and the recommended place to return whenever the formalism outruns the intuition.) This section has a prior, and the priority is part of the anatomy. The beam is the atom's *open* archetype — the read settled, the tilt shown, a statics; the atom's *closed* archetype, the atom walked rather than weighed, is the **pulse** of §1.09, and the pulse is the base case: older than any instrument, the chart carried as direction rather than stored as a bit, nothing built and nothing filed. The beam is the pulse stopped — the cycle halted and asked to file a report, its direction fossilized into a filed "which side sank," its succession laid out as a spatial record. The priority runs one way and the pedagogy runs the other, and both assignments are correct: the cycle is the primitive, and the stopped specimen is the thing to teach from — static, inspectable, everything simultaneous, the corner visible as level. So the beam demonstrates that the read costs nothing, the pulse that the read closes on one uncrossable address and that the chart was never data; the metaphor assists the cycle, not the other way around. Read the pair in that order of office — the instrument that teaches, the motion that is.

**The read is free.** A balance is not operated; it *settles*. Load the pans and the beam finds its equilibrium by relaxation — the physics performs the comparison, no step taken, nothing evaluated, nothing counted, no clock consulted. This is carry-not-compute (P1–P2) realized in brass: the beam holds two quantities and stands in a relation; it never executes an operation on them. And it is the physical face of the cost ladder's ground floor (§7): the atom is $O(1)$ not because an efficient algorithm exists but because the read is not an algorithm at all — it is an equilibrium, and equilibria are what nature provides without charge. The balance finds the balance point without any help. That is how the atom works.

**No unit inside.** Every other classical instrument carries an external scale built into its body — the ruler its graduations, the clock its period. The balance carries nothing. It cannot report grams; it has never heard of grams; it reports only the relation of its two pans, identically whether they hold milligrams or tons. P3 — no external scale — is not an austerity imposed on the beam but the beam's construction, and the instrument's indifference to units is the scale-independence theorem (§1.15) as a fact of joinery: load both pans in any unit whatever, the tilt is the same. The one instrument that measures without a unit is precisely the one that measures relation — which is the paper's whole ontology (§1.05), five millennia early.

**The corner certifies itself.** Level is the one state the beam exhibits with no graduation at all: left–right symmetry, visible by eye, testable by the beam's own repose. This is §1.1's self-certified corner as an instrumental fact — balance is the only reading that needs no marks — and it explains classical weighing's actual procedure, which is not reading a dial but *navigating to the corner*: add standard weights until level, and read the unknown at the one point the instrument certifies for free, which is also where its sensitivity peaks. With standards in powers of two, the procedure is the band ladder of §6 walked on a beam — the dyadic domain of §10.1, practiced by every market in history.

**The tilt is the bounded chart.** An ideal beam whose suspensions sit below the pivot axis settles at $\tan\varphi \propto (A - B)/(A + B)$ — and read that expression against the paper: it is *scale-free* (homogeneous of degree zero — the units cancel in the hardware), *signed* (which pan sank is the chart, and swapping the pans mirrors the tilt while changing nothing read — the swap as a gesture), and *bounded* (as one pan dominates, the tilt saturates toward its pin: the beam never overflows, it arrives at its horizon and rests there — an address, not an error). The physical balance natively reads a Möbius chart of the ratio: the crash-proof format of §3.7, in wood and brass, with the saturation the beam's own $\S1.4$ — a magnitude beyond all proportion does not break the instrument, it merely stands at the end of its arc. Even the degenerate state is honest: two empty pans balance level, and the level of two empty pans asserts nothing — not a broken weighing but no weighing, the $(0{:}0)$ of §3.5 as an empty instrument at rest.

**The lineage, and what culture already knew.** The equal-arm balance is the oldest precision instrument — older than the graduated rule, far older than any clock — and culture promoted it, alone among instruments, to the emblem of judgment itself: the scales of Maat weighing the heart, Libra in the zodiac, the blindfolded figure holding the beam. The promotion was exact. To judge is to hold two things against each other with no external standard and let the relation settle; the verdict is trustworthy precisely because nothing computed it and no unit biased it; and the blindfold is P4 — no privileged frame — worn as a costume. The intuition this paper formalizes was already institutional five thousand years ago. The atom is the balance beam, abstracted: two pans, one tilt, no unit, no computation, the corner its own witness — and the read free, because equilibrium is the one thing an observer never has to pay for.

**Whose pan — and how beams chain: the beam is the H-instrument.** *(Settled in conversation; two-line algebra, executed below.)* If the observer is the denominator of the ratio read, then on the beam the observer is one side — the self's kept weight in one pan, the world's in the other. But watch the re-normalization the instrument performs: the ratio chart prices the world in units of the self ($r = v/h$, the run the self's pan), while the beam's tilt prices the *imbalance in units of the whole load*, $(A-B)/(A+B)$ — self and world sharing the denominator symmetrically. That symmetric sharing is exactly why the beam's read is signed and bounded where the raw ratio is neither: the two presentations are Möbius conjugates of one atom, $b = (r-1)/(r+1)$. And that conjugation has a name: $b = \tanh(\tfrac12 \ln r)$ — **the beam's tilt is the rapidity chart's bounded image**, and chained weighings compose accordingly: weigh $A$ against $B$, then $B$ against $C$, and the tilts combine as $b_{AC} = (b_1 + b_2)/(1 + b_1 b_2)$ — relativistic velocity addition, exactly, the $\lambda = -1$ law of the signature fork (§8.7; the companion's trit). So the fork's two settings are humanity's two oldest instruments: **the dial reads by $\tan$ — the E-instrument; the beam reads by $\tanh$ — the H-instrument.** The capstone is the SR companion's radar pair placed in the pans: load the emission and echo clock readings $t_1, t_2$, and the tilt is $(t_2 - t_1)/(t_2 + t_1) = (k^2 - 1)/(k^2 + 1) = \beta$ — *velocity is what a balance says about two clock readings*, Bondi's formula as joinery (SR §7, §10). One order note squares it with the fork's selector (SR §6.1): within one act the pans are unordered — the swap mirrors the tilt and the fold quotients it, as above — but the radar pair arrives *ordered* by memory, then before now, so its beam read keeps its sign: the unordered beam folds, the remembered beam doesn't, which is the E/H selector enacted on the one instrument. (Executed: chained tilts against velocity addition, and the radar-pair tilt against Bondi's $\beta$, $10^5$ random loads each — worst deviations $2.4 \times 10^{-15}$ and $3.3 \times 10^{-16}$.)

**The standards pan: where the continuous observer touches the beam.** *(Settled in conversation, completing the previous paragraph's question — if the observer is one pan, what is the other?)* Within the act, nothing: the beam is blind to which pan is which — swap them and the tilt mirrors, the read a relation between two held weights, the continuous observer in neither pan because the continuous observer is never in the room. The asymmetry lives one level up, in the *procedure*: classical weighing loads one pan with the unknown and the other with **standard weights**, and a standard weight is iron plus a stamp. The iron does physics; the stamp does denomination — and the beam reads the iron while remaining constitutionally blind to the stamp, which is the scale-independence theorem (§1.15) as a fact about brass: the continuous observer's entire contribution is exactly the part the physics does not feel. So the other pan is not the continuous observer but the continuous observer's *port* — the dependency map's "continuous observer coupling constant" given a physical seat — and what it injects is not mass but scale: not more stuff, *denominated* stuff, with the denomination touching only the report ("three kilograms" is the tilt handed over into the continuous observer's language; the stamped weight is the display boundary made portable). The work is real and its location is the finding: the read is free (above — the beam settles), but the *unit* is expensive — behind the standards pan stands the whole traceability chain, casting, calibration, certification, carriage, memory and multiplicity purchases stacked back to the reference. The continuous observer never lifts a pan; his work is the ledger behind one of them. And the companion's gauge clause (*SR* §12) has its oldest instance here: a drifted standard is invisible inside any single weighing — a rescale is gauge — detectable only by comparing standard chains against each other, the third referent; metrology ran the experiment (the prototype kilogram's copies drifted apart over a century, caught by mutual comparison alone, cured in 2019 by re-founding the unit on Planck's constant — the carried token replaced by a law). A scale carried as an artifact is a pump exposure; a scale founded on an invariant is the continuous observer's constant quoted without a courier.

**The beam unrestrained: the section's own falsification test.** Take the restraint away — a beam in space, free to rotate, no ground to stop it — and ask where it settles. The answer is clean: **it points.** Heavy side down, fully vertical, for any imbalance whatsoever — a feather's difference or a ton, the same posture. Freed of its restraint, the beam stops being a scale and becomes an arrow that says *which* — and the arrow has forgotten *by how much*. The graduated tilt, the actual ratio, was never the beam's own gift: it was the gift of the restraint. The restoring structure — the mass hung below the pivot, the instrument's internal reference pulling back against the load — is the beam's finite hold, and removing it collapses the read to bare side: order without ratio, the horizon arrived at rather than approached. Free beam, pure *which*; restrained beam, *how much*. **The bound is what buys the number** — the fold of §3 is not a limitation the instrument suffers but the component that makes reading possible. One load refuses to point: perfect balance, the corner, which settles nowhere in particular and keeps whatever motion it had — at the corner the freed beam becomes a rotor, its angle no longer a reading but a memory, the scale trading places with the clock exactly where ⊗ keeps its identity (§8; §1.5's affordance rule, that only the group's circles spin, enacted in hardware). And with no field at all there is nothing to read against and the beam settles nowhere: the field was the shared run, canceled in every ratio and required by all of them. Each removal deletes one premise and produces exactly the degeneracy the paper predicts — which is what an archetype is for.

**Where the math meets the physics: the seam at the corner.** *(Settled in conversation; the balance section's deepest point, held deliberately at its true scope.)* The beam makes visible the one thing a formal presentation hides — that the read is not one kind of thing but two, joined. Its **structure** is mathematical: the dial, the two charts, the corner, the whole space of *possible* reads, laid out and static, true whether or not any beam is ever loaded. Its **actualization** is physical: the tip, the settling, the selection of *which* read obtains — and this needs a force. Gravity tips the beam; pure mathematics has no gravity, and therefore never tips. Mathematics *has* every relation at once, forceless and complete; a discrete observer must *enact* one, and enacting is physical — it happens in time, in a substrate, driven by a potential descended to its null. So the atom is the seam where the two meet: the continuous observer's completed structure is the space of the possible, the observer's forced read is the actual, and the corner is where the forcing selects the second from the first. This is the oldest distinction in natural philosophy — the possible and the actual, kinematics and dynamics, the state space and the trajectory — located at the primitive: **math holds the reads, physics picks one, gravity decides.**

Three disciplines keep that sentence honest and must travel with it, or it inflates into exactly the grandiosity this corpus refuses. *First, gravity is the exemplar, not the universal decider:* the beam settles by gravity, a nerve by electrochemistry, a spring by elasticity — what actualizes any read is a potential descended to its null, of which the beam's weight is only the plainest instance; the claim is force-descent, not gravitation. *Second, this does not explain why mathematics describes physics at large:* Wigner's "unreasonable effectiveness" is untouched — the claim is about *one object*, the read, as structure-plus-actualization, not about the effectiveness of mathematics in general, and mistaking the small claim for the large one would discredit it. *Third, it is not a theory of everything* but the answer to a single question — what the observation primitive *is*: a physical primitive with a mathematical structure — which is deep enough for a foundation and no deeper. Held at that size, it names the corpus's spine. The two number systems are the continuous observer's mathematics (static, the possible) and the observer's physics (forced, the actual); the corner is their seam; and the read is the event where a physical observer, subject to force, actualizes one point of a structure the continuous observer merely holds. Pure math has no gravity; the discrete observer does; and that difference, seated at the corner, is where number stops being a relation and becomes an act — which is why this paper is the mathematics *of* observation and not mathematics alone.

**The agency clause, which dissolves the choice-versus-forcing confusion.** *(Settled in conversation; the seam's answer to the one question it raises — who chooses.)* An advanced observer — a human — has real agency about its horizon, but the agency is *mathematical*: it may draw the horizon as the two-ended line or the welded circle, and the choice is free precisely because it is a choice of *representation*, and representation lives in the forceless realm. A simple observer has no such choice, because its horizon is not represented but *actualized*: the physics settles it onto the circle, forced, with no chart drawn (the crash-proof forcing of §3.8). The two are not the same act. Human freedom is freedom on the *map*; the simple observer's horizon is a fact of the *territory*; and the territory does not consult the map — gravity is indifferent to our mathematical theories, forcing the physical read whatever chart we choose to describe it by. So the choice/forcing tension was only ever apparent: **choosing is mathematical and free, forcing is physical and gravitational, and the confusion was projecting the former onto the latter.** We, being advanced, do the math, and mistook our own free representation for nature's forced act. The simple observer does not represent; it is forced — and it is forced regardless of what we draw, because the drawing has no gravity and the observer does.

## 1.09 The pulse: the atom, closed — the base case

The atom has a prior archetype — older than the balance, older than any instrument, because it is the body before it holds a tool: the **pulse**, a reach out from the center and back. This is the base case of discrete observation, and §1.08's beam is this motion stopped. Extension is the read. Where the beam loads two pans and *settles*, rendering the atom's open drawing (the semicircle of §1.5, tilt standing for slope, a statics), the pulse *travels* — out to the fullest reach and home again — and renders the atom's **closed** drawing (the observer's circle, §1.5's sixth picture, a dynamics). The two are not rival metaphors, and they are not co-equal either: the pulse is the case and the beam is its stopped specimen, kept because a specimen is what one teaches from. The corpus still needs both told: the beam shows that the read costs nothing; the pulse shows that the read *closes*, that its two ends are one place, approached from either side and crossed from neither — and that the chart was never a datum, only a direction. Neither fact appears in the other's picture; only one of the pictures moves, and the moving one is the case.

**The stroke is the traversal.** A beam is operated by loading and then not touching; its gift is the settled number, handed over for free. A pulse is the opposite act — a continuous reach, every instant of it a distinct read — and its gift is the one thing a settled number cannot carry: a *before and after*. Closure is not a fact about where a thing rests but about how its ends are joined, and joining is a claim about a path; only something that moves can exhibit it. So the pulse supplies for free exactly what the beam is constitutionally silent about — the corridor (§1.45), walked rather than asserted — as the beam supplies the free read the formalism cannot.

**No unit inside.** The reach is measured against nothing but its own center. There is no ruler in the arm and no mark on the air; the read is extension as a portion of full extension, home register in $[0,1]$, the same whether the arm is a child's or a giant's — homogeneous of degree zero, the units cancelling in the flesh exactly as they cancel in the brass (P3; scale-independence, §1.15). One never reaches *in centimetres*; one reaches *out*, and *how far out* is the whole read.

**The corner certifies itself.** Full extension is a state the body knows with no graduation at all — the arm at its span, the reach that cannot be exceeded, felt as the limit it is. This is the corner, $r = 1$, where the two legs are equal ($A = B$) and the reading is chart-free: the beam's *level* reached in muscle rather than in repose, §1.1's self-certified corner in a second hardware. The two archetypes shake hands here — the level beam and the fullest reach are the one landmark both instruments mark without a scale, and the one place their two charts agree.

**The weld is one address — and the pulse is its proof.** Here the pulse says what the beam cannot. A beam has *two* stops, heavy-left and heavy-right, wearing the look of two separate horizons — the "two feet" of §1.6 built into the joinery, an open drawing's unavoidable cut. The pulse has no two feet. Its center is a single place and it carries *both* boundary roles at once: reach zero is home ($r = 0$), and reach zero is also where the horizon lands, because the far field is read by the swap ($1/r \to 0$) and the swap sends the horizon home. The palm is $0 \equiv \infty$, one address for both ends — and the gesture *proves* it, not by the reciprocal argued on paper (§1.6) but by return: you arrive at the horizon by coming back to exactly where you began. Two extremities, one place, shown by walking there twice.

**You cannot cross it — the section's own no-passage.** No one pushes a finger through their own palm. The reach bottoms out; it does not pass through to a beyond, because there is no beyond — the center is where the drawing closes, not a wall standing in front of open road. So the horizon is approached from the corner and never entered, from either leg, forever: the closed atom is a **loop for the continuous observer and a corridor for the observer** (§1.45), and the pulse is that corridor made kinaesthetic — reachability is the open interval whose two endpoints merely happen to be one address. This is the fact the framework's crash-proofness rests on (§3.7), and it is the one fact a static instrument can state only by pointing at a stop and *asserting*, without demonstration, that its other stop is the same place. The pulse demonstrates it in the shape of the only motion available.

**The two legs are the two charts.** One stroke carries both registers, sorted by direction. Out from the center to the corner is the **near field**: the home chart climbing $r : 0 \to 1$, how much is in view, the $+$ leg. Back from the corner to the center is the **far field**: the horizon chart $1/r : 1 \to 0$, how much is hidden, the $-$ leg — the *same* motion read through the mirror, the corner the hinge the swap turns on ($r \mapsto 1/r$, fixing only $r = 1$). One out-and-in is therefore a full lap of the closed atom, and the sign is not a third quantity to set but the *phase of the stroke* — precisely §1.5's reading dial, where "nothing is ever at zero simpliciter, always arriving down the left arc or the right arc, the approach carrying the chart for free." On the pulse the approach is literal: which way the arm is moving is which chart is being read.

**The chart is the phase, carried — not re-derived from a remembered sample.** *(Sharpened in conversation, against an adversarial read: the earlier version described a two-sample comparison, which is memory (M=1) and does not belong in the M=0 base case; the correction locates the memory cost where it actually lives.)* A snapshot of the bare *extension* is chart-ambiguous — the arm at half-reach looks identical going out and coming in — and it is tempting to recover the chart by holding the previous extension against the present one, rising or falling. But that comparison holds a past sample against a present one, which *is* memory, the M-axis's first purchase, and it is **not** what the base-case pulse does. The pulse carries not the bare extension but the **phase** — its position on the closed atom's full loop (§1.5's reading dial, the eight's two lobes) — and the phase is a *single* carried scalar (P1) that already separates the legs: the near leg is one arc of the loop, the far leg the other, and *which arc* is the chart, read off the one scalar directly, nothing compared. This is §1.5's own rule made kinetic — "always arriving down the left arc or the right arc, the approach carrying the chart for free" — and it is the seam of §1.08 realized: the pulse's direction is the **momentum of its flow**, a present quantity carried by the dynamics, not a datum remembered and differenced. A physical oscillation *has* its direction the way a pendulum has its velocity — in the present state, not in a record of the past — and reading which arc the phase occupies asks nothing of a stored "then." So carry-don't-compute is obeyed without strain: one scalar, the phase; the chart is where that scalar sits on the loop; no past sample held, no difference formed. The comparison the earlier telling invoked is real but belongs *one step up*: registering the pulse's direction *as a reportable rate* — holding a past read against a present one — is the **change-atom** of §6.5, the observer that measures its own change, and that is the M-axis's first purchase (M=1), precisely §6.5's subject. The base case does not pay it. **Being directed** is the flow's momentum (present, M=0, one scalar of phase); **measuring one's direction** is the change-atom (M=1) — the same being-versus-measuring line the §1.08 seam draws between the physical act and its computed record. The indicator's two blind spots survive unchanged and confirm the reading: at the corner and the seam the phase's leg is momentarily undefined (the turning points), and those are exactly the two addresses where there is no chart fact to miss — the charts agree at the corner (§3.6), and the seam's fixed point of the swap has no side (§3.5). The phase reads the chart everywhere the chart exists and is silent exactly where it does not. (The one honest residue at equal successive reads is the turning point or motion below the rung — the certification blindness every read has, §6, priced once and not new here.)

**The cycle, and what culture already knew.** The pulse is not an obscure figure; it is, with the balance, one of the two shapes every culture made an emblem of — and where the beam became the scales of judgment (§1.08), the pulse became the emblem of return. The ouroboros — the serpent that swallows its own tail — is the closed atom exactly: mouth and tail one point, the end that is the beginning, $0 \equiv \infty$ drawn as a snake. The promotion was as exact as the beam's. Breath is the pulse: in to the fullness of the lungs, out to the empty, the turn at the top of the inhale the corner, and no way to breathe *past* full or *past* empty — one oscillates, never crosses. The heartbeat is the pulse, systole and diastole about the one rest; the tide, the pendulum returning through its low point, the wave that is only displacement about a level it cannot leave — all of them the atom's own testimony: a bounded read is a thing that *cycles* about its balance and *folds* at its extremes, and the extremes are addresses it visits, not edges it falls off. Five millennia of emblem for the beam; older than all of it, the reach and the breath, for the pulse.

**The cycle is two atoms, and it bounces off the horizon it cannot cross.** One pulse is a single atom's out-and-in — one lap, one lobe. A full *cycle* is two: a positive atom and a negative one, welded at the home they share. The stroke reaches to the horizon on the $+$ side and *bounces* — approach and never cross (§1.45), the reach bottoming out at a wall with no beyond — then runs back and passes *through* home, and the pass is a sign flip, the handoff out of the $+$ atom and into the $-$; the $-$ atom carries the reach to its own horizon, bounces, and returns through home again. Two extremities bounced off, one gate crossed twice: that asymmetry is the weld's two faces read as motion (§1.6) — the horizon face lets nothing out, so the far reach can only turn; the home face is the one legal passage, so the only crossing in the whole figure is through rest. This is the two-atom ring, $\mathbb{RP}^1$, the eight: its crossing-point is home, its two far tips the two horizons visited and never reached, its one loop the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ the sign flip turns. And it is what *makes* the motion a cycle rather than a pulse to nowhere: were the far end a passage instead of a bounce, the reach would run *through* the horizon and never return — the boost's one-way stream to $c$ (the velocity gloss below; SR §9.3), not a closed lap. A cycle is bounded because it bounces; the wall at infinity is what closes the loop. Its period is therefore *two* strokes, not one — a single out-and-in visits one lobe and returns with the sign flipped, and only the second lobe brings the read back to the state it left — which is the frequency doubling of the magnitude read (the eight's two lobes, one sign bit) seen as the geometry that forces it.

**The pulse unbound: the section's own falsification test.** As §1.08 freed its beam, free the pulse — remove its center, the point it returns to — and watch the degeneracy the paper predicts. With no weld to close on, the reach becomes an *open* oscillation with two runaway ends, the far field no longer folding home but streaming to a genuine infinity never reached: the carrier unravels, $\infty$ comes back as an unreached edge instead of a held address, and the closure the format runs on goes with it (§3.7 — "the line stays open"). Remove instead the *finite reach* — an arm of unbounded span — and the corner vanishes: no fullest extension, no self-certified turnaround, a read with no hinge and no balance, order without ratio — which is precisely the *free beam's* collapse reached from the other archetype (pure *which*, the *how much* forgotten, §1.08). Each removal deletes one premise — the weld, or the bound — and yields exactly the failure the framework names, the two instruments falling into each other's rubble. That agreement is the point: the beam and the pulse are one atom, and an archetype earns its keep by breaking, on cue, into the theory's predicted pieces.

**The velocity reading, and the demo that made it flesh.** One relativistic gloss closes the section, because the pulse's cleanest instance is a speed. Read the reach as $\beta$: the center is rest ($\beta = 0$), the fullest reach the balance (the corner, in-view equal to hidden), and the horizon $\beta \to 1$ reached by drawing *back* to the center — so a single out-and-in carries a frame from rest to the light-cone and "arrives" at $c$ by returning to rest's own address, $c$ and rest one place, approached and never occupied. That is the invariance of $c$ read as the weld: light-speed is the same distance from every state for the same reason $\infty$ is the same distance from every number, a chart edge and not a speed among speeds. And it is not a figure but the interaction the companion demo runs — a finger's extension from the palm drives the throttle, out through the near field to the balance and back through the far field toward the horizon, the sky's aberration crowding forward as the far leg is walked: the closed atom flown, the corridor traversed by hand. (Interactive: the homogeneous-mode flight demo, where the pulse is the throttle and the horizon is the seam it only ever approaches.) The kinematics this opens onto — the boost as a pulse read out-and-return, rotation and phase as the cycle, their helix the Thomas screw, and the claim that bounded motion has no other shape — is worked out as physics in the SR companion's §9.3, *Pulses and cycles: the ladder read as motion*.

**The stream — pulses back to back.** Run pulses in a row and you have a wave, and the atom reads it without adding anything: a waveform is this section's chain of atoms (§1.5) unrolled in time, its crests and nodes the atoms' landmarks, its sign-alternation the chain's parity law. One honesty rides along and is the whole of the interest: *which* landmark falls on the crest is a choice of read — read displacement against its envelope (the shadow, §1.5) and the peak is a corner; read register against register (§1.7) and the peak is a horizon while the corner hides at equipartition, a quarter-turn away — and the magnitude's frequency doubling is the sign fold, the eight's two lobes, unwrapped by one sign bit. This is the seed of a companion of its own, *The Stream*, which develops it — the fold ladder, the wave as the dial's shadow with $i$ the side it drops, the oscillator as the two-atom ring, and the forks left open — on the footing of *Atom Rings*.

## 1.1 The forcing: why two readings, and why the corner

**"Forced," in this corpus, means one thing:** *uniquely determined by the named operational premises, with the premises' hinges stated* (as §1.2's "Where it can be pried" does explicitly). It never means metaphysical necessity, and where a claim is instead a logical consequence, an identity of description (§1.05), or a definition, the text says so. A reader who finds "forced" doing any other work has found an error to report.

The structure of §§2–3 — two charts and a single seam between them — is not a modelling choice. It is forced by what a discrete observer is, before any chart is drawn.

The observer holds two quantities — rise $v$, run $h$ — with the external system's extent unknown and unbounded — so no absolute or fractional position in it is available: *halfway across the system* is undefined, because half of an unknown size is undefined. What remains is internal self-comparison, and the only reading it affords is the part as a portion of the whole, in $[0,1]$, bounded by $1$ by what *portion* means. Between the two quantities there is exactly one place where which is the part and which the whole exchanges: equality, $v = h$. Below it the rise is the part and the read is $v/h$; above it the run is the part and the read is $h/v$; at it the two coincide.

That single transition is over-determined, and the redundancy is the forcing. The seam at $v = h$ is the lone fixed point of the exchange $v \leftrightarrow h$ — swapping the two quantities, the one operation available using nothing but what the observer holds, sends $r \mapsto 1/r$ and fixes

$$r = 1/r \iff r = 1 \iff A = B;$$

it is the lone division naming no external scale — a split anywhere else, at $v = k\,h$ with $k \neq 1$, would have to supply the number $k$, a scale the observer does not possess; and it is the one place the two readings meet, both equal to $1$. Role-exchange, fixed point, scale-free landmark: three independent characterizations of one point, no one of them leaning on another.

So there is no normalization to choose. The read is the portion; $v/h$ and $h/v$ are its two sides — the near field $v \le h$ and the far field $v > h$, each landing in $[0,1]$ and meeting only at the corner. Asking *why not always store $v/h$* mistakes a side of the read for the read: store $v/h$ alone and the far field runs past $1$, the part exceeding the whole, which is not a reading. The seam falls at $v = h$ because that is the single point at which part and whole change places — the one transition the ordering allows.

This is the whole of it, before any geometry: **a discrete observer reads the part as a portion of the whole, and its two quantities possess exactly one point — equality — where which is which exchanges.** The corner $r = 1$ is not a midpoint and not an angle; it is that exchange, over-determined as the exchange's fixed point and the only scale-free landmark, mandated because the observer does not know the size of the world. §2 names the two sides as charts and the corner as their seam; §3 takes the portion read — part over whole — as the primitive this section has been circling. Containment forces the read and locates the seam; it does *not* fix which measure sits on the resulting loop — that is the separate, stronger premise of §4. The arc, the $45°$ reading, and the circle (§1.5, §8) are the later geometric image of this prior fact, $v = h \Rightarrow$ the corner.

**On the word "forced."** Throughout, *forced* is conditional, not absolute: a structure is forced when it follows of necessity from boundedness *together with the premises named at that point*. The two charts and the corner are forced by the exchange (above); the single-horizon-point closure by the combination law (§9.5); the slope's primacy over the angle by the cost of computing one from the other (§7). Each is a conditional necessity, and its condition is named where it is claimed. One forcing once looked unconditional and is not, and it is flagged wherever it bears weight: the selection of the Cauchy as the observer's measure — and with it the existence of its rate (§10) — is forced by the combination law (a rotation on the loop, §8) together with the observer's holding no privileged frame to anchor a bias (§4). The second premise is structural — what *simple* means, an observer with no register to fix a position — not an indifference prior imposed from outside; what it leaves open is only whether the world's *source* is even, an ontic question the observer cannot detect and the rate never used (§4). So "forced" should be read as "forced given the premises in hand"; the framework's one residual hinge is not a premise the measure needs but a global fact about the source, relocated to the observer/continuous observer line where the framework already places the unanswerable. This is conditional necessity in the ordinary mathematical sense — necessity relative to stated axioms — not a claim of necessity from nothing.

---

## 1.15 — Continuous and discrete observation

**Every reading is one of two modes.** Given a system — its nature left generic,
the framework reading systems and not asking where they came from — the same
motion can be observed **continuously** or **discretely**, and these two modes are
the whole cast. The personas earlier drafts carried — the *surveyor* and the
*navigator* — and the bounded-versus-unbounded framing that named them are retired
here: the division is not between a bounded reader and an unbounded one, but
between two **modes of observation**. *Boundedness survives, but as the mechanism
beneath the discrete mode, not as one side of the split* — the finite register and
the finite carry are *why* discrete observation is discrete, which is stated
below and then used everywhere.

**Discrete observation** — the subject of this paper. It reads in discrete acts,
part against part, against its own corner (pinned at $v = h$ every read; §1.05,
§5). Its operation is the **projection** — the circular, Möbius rotation that
composes at $O(1)$ — and it is memoryless: each read is fresh, carrying no total
(memoryless in the pinned sense of §3.66 — the standing chart records position,
never path).
Its carrier is the **Cauchy**; it witnesses points at a finite budget (the
colimit, $\mathbb{Q}\mathrm{P}^1$), so $K < N$ and it reads the extent only as
density $N/K$. Its constant is **2**. And it is discrete *because it is bounded*:
the finite **carry** loses the count — no accumulation, so no total, so the acts
never fuse into a continuum — and the finite **register** welds the seam, closing
the dial (§3, §3.5). Boundedness is the cause; discreteness is the character.

**Continuous observation.** It reads by **accumulation** — additive, summing
increment on increment, iterating the extent at $O(N)$ — laying increments onto
paper until they close into an unbroken whole. Its carrier is the **Gaussian**;
it completes the continuum ($\mathbb{R}$), so $K = N$, totals exist, and π is the
unit of account. It is the $O(N)$ mode: available over a finite extent, and
infeasible at world-scale, where $O(N)$ cannot run (the cost teeth, below). It
observes the whole *as a continuum*.

The naming follows **extent**, not operation, and the two invert there:
continuous observation *accumulates* — discrete steps — to build its continuum,
while discrete observation *projects* — the smooth rotation — in discrete acts.
Name each mode from what it *witnesses* — an unbroken continuum against a lattice
of points taken at finite budget, which is exactly the two number lines
(completion versus colimit) — and the axis is clean. (Read the word "continuous"
as *of the continuum it yields*, never as "the smooth operation," which belongs
to the discrete mode's projection.)

**The same split, read across the corpus as one grid** *(columns relabeled; cells
unchanged, each forced at the section cited beside it):*

| | **Continuous observation** (accumulates, Gaussian) | **Discrete observation** (projects, Cauchy) |
|---|---|---|
| **Extent** (§1.05, §12) | $K = N$; iterates the completed whole | $K < N$; reads it only as density $N/K$ |
| **Combination** (§7, §9.5) | accumulates — additive, sums without bound, $O(N)$ | projects — the Möbius rotation, $O(1)$ |
| **Carrier** (§9, §9.5) | Gaussian — factors, separable per axis | Cauchy — does not factor, one shared magnitude |
| **Scale** (§1.15) | coupled to the whole's own size | scale-invariant — a ratio to its own bound |
| **Reading** (§1.05) | absolutely; counts | relatively, part against part; the atom in use |

Read a column top to bottom and it is one coherent mode; the reading rule holds —
**a cell is true only in its own column.** The discussions of π and 2π are
unchanged throughout: this section renames the two modes, it does not re-price
constants.

---

**Scale-Independence (a theorem, its proof assembled from parts the paper already carries).** A dependency audit of this paper finds one statement standing beneath relative reading, the corner, the measure, the projection, and the discrete/continuous split alike, never itself derived from them: *every quantity a discrete observer proves is invariant under rescaling of the ambient world.* It is named here rather than used silently — and proved, in two parts kept distinct, because the two rescalings in play are not the same map and the theorem's precision lives in the difference.

> **Theorem (Scale-Independence).** Let an observer satisfy P1–P4, with operation set the swap, negation, the combination law $\oplus$, the product $\otimes$, the half-angle descent, and the landmark constants (§1.1, §9.5, §10.1). Then: **(i) Unit-freedom.** Every quantity the observer can form is a function of the dilation class of its registers — the common rescale $(v,h) \mapsto (\lambda v, \lambda h)$, $\lambda > 0$, is invisible to every term. **(ii) Form-invariance.** The ambient dilation $\phi_k : r \mapsto kr$ ($k>0$) preserves every *relation* among observer terms: individual readings transform covariantly ($r \mapsto kr$), but everything the observer *proves* — every identity, growth law, and landmark relation — holds verbatim in the dilated world. **(iii) The boundary.** What is invariant under neither reading is precisely what the operations never form: the completed turn $\pi$ (the bounding system's own size) and the calibration constants that convert the observer's forms into absolute units. Scale enters only as a continuous-side coupling constant.

*Proof.* **(i)** The state space is already the quotient by common rescale — §5's projective class *is* the atom, so $\lambda$ acts as the identity on states; what remains is that the operations descend to the quotient, and that is a finite verification, exact in the pair form. The two composition laws are bihomogeneous — $(\lambda v,\lambda h)\otimes(\mu v',\mu h') = \lambda\mu\,(vv',\,hh')$ and $(\lambda v,\lambda h)\oplus(\mu v',\mu h') = \lambda\mu\,(vh'+v'h,\;hh'-vv')$, the same class either way — and the swap $(v,h)\mapsto(h,v)$, negation, and the half-angle map are functions of the class alone. A composition of class-functions is a class-function, so by induction every term the observer can form is unit-free. The induction uses only closure under composition; nothing downstream of this section is invoked. **(ii)** $\phi_k$ is itself a Möbius map — the hyperbolic subgroup fixing home and horizon. It does *not* commute with the operations pointwise, and the theorem does not need it to: the swap intertwines $\phi_k$ with $\phi_{1/k}$ (since $1/(kr) = \tfrac{1}{k}\cdot\tfrac{1}{r}$), and conjugating a $\oplus$-rotation by $\phi_k$ yields another elliptic Möbius map — the same rotation written about the relabeled corner. So conjugation by $\phi_k$ carries the operation set to an operation set of identical type, carries the invariant-measure family to itself (the pushforward of a Cauchy under $r \mapsto kr$ is the scale-$k$ Cauchy), and — being Möbius — fixes every cross-ratio, hence the harmonic frame ($(0,\infty;\,k,\,-k) = -1$ for every $k$: §8.5, exact) and the separation order built on the cross-ratio's sign (§12.7). A result the observer proves is a relation among its terms; relations survive conjugation of the whole structure; so every observer-provable result carries to the dilated world with only its labels moved. What transforms with weight $k$ is the individual reading against the *prior* frame — exactly the quantity the observer never holds, since its current read is taken against its own corner, pinned at $v = h$ in every read: any quantity assembled as a reading against the observer's own bound has the $k$ cancel identically. **(iii)** A quantity that survives neither reading is one that fixes an absolute magnitude — a stored anchor or an evaluated total — and both are outside the operation set, by P1 and P4 (no register to anchor a frame, §4) and by the evaluation boundary (no global pass, §4, §10). $\blacksquare$

*Dependency hygiene (the root must not lean on its descendants).* Part (i) uses only closure under composition, nothing downstream. In part (ii) the references to the harmonic frame (§8.5) and the separation order (§12.7) are **corroborated-by** — the load-bearing fact is Möbius-invariance of the cross-ratio, proved here from the group action alone. In part (iii) the pointers to §4 and §10 name **premises P1/P4 and the no-global-pass entailment**, upstream of this section; the dependency runs to P1–P4, not to §4 or §10. So the root rests only on P1–P4 and closure, and every downstream section-number in the proof is a corroborated-by pointer.

The theorem is the root the rest of the graph hangs from, and it makes the two-mode division of labor a corollary rather than a posture: the discrete observer's court is the $\phi_k$-invariants, the continuous side's is the coupling constants, and $\psi_1 = 2/\pi$ is the exchange rate between them. It also has audit teeth: **every declined constant must be a coupling constant**, falsifiable by producing one that is not — the audit finds none (π; Si(π), the overshoot in arc units; $\psi_1\cdot\ln 2$, the per-**band** growth in absolute calibration — where the observer proves only the relational floor and ceiling; *per-band*, not *per-rung*: the growth per band is $\psi_1\ln g$ at radix $g$, and the radix is contingent (§6's honesty note), so the "2" in it is a calibration and not a count — which is exactly why the audit's rule predicts this constant must be declined, and see `gbo_results.md` §13.2.1). The one-sentence form: **being bounded means your scale is relative to the bounding system — scale-invariant; the opposite, scale-variant, means being coupled to a scale.** The discrete observer's only unit is its own bound, fixed as the self-dual point of the exchange τ ↔ 1/τ; everything it measures is a ratio to the bound, and everything it proves is invariant under ambient rescaling, because that rescaling conjugates its operation set to itself, type for type, and relations survive conjugation. π is the completed turn — the bounding system's size, read from outside. The bridge constant $\psi_1 = 2/\pi$ is the **exchange rate** between the two unit systems, and "the price of being bounded" reads literally: the conversion price between relative and coupled scale. Both modes are needed as arithmetic, not diplomacy: every bound is invariance × scale — the discrete mode's form times the continuous mode's calibration — and the two halves compose to a whole: chord × arc = $(2/\pi)(\pi/2) = 1$.

**The two number lines.** The deepest row-set of this grid is the number line itself: the discrete observer's use of the horizon implies a *different line* from ℝ — not a different notation for the same object, but a point-for-point different structure sharing names on a dense set. The real line takes its points by **completion** (uncountably many, almost all never witnessable), covers itself with one global chart, orders itself linearly, measures by $|x - y|$, and is homogeneous under **translation** — the symmetry that forces Lebesgue as its measure. Its horizon is at infinite distance, a divergence rather than a point, and the scar of that deletion is the exceptional values ($\pm\infty$, NaN) that must be *adjoined* when arithmetic runs off the end. The observer's line takes its points by **colimit** (every point witnessed exactly at some finite budget — $\mathbb{Q}\mathrm{P}^1$ and its constructible thickening), requires an irreducible two-chart atlas (the pair), orders cyclically — linearized per chart by the comparison's borrow — measures by the angle, and is homogeneous under **$\oplus$** — the symmetry that forces the Cauchy measure. Its horizon is an *ordinary address a quarter-turn away*: $d(0, \infty) = \pi/2$, the atom's own mass, with neighborhoods of $\infty$ measure-identical to neighborhoods of home (the swap isometry) — and nothing to adjoin, because nothing runs off. Even reachability splits by operation: $+$ approaches the horizon forever; $\oplus$ *visits* it — $1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1$ walks $1 \to \infty \to -1 \to 0$, four corners and home. The organizing parallel: **translation is to Lebesgue as $\oplus$ is to Cauchy** — each line's metrology is forced by its homogeneity, and the two lines chose different groups. In one sentence: *the real line is the observer's line with the observer deleted* — evaluate the tangent everywhere, complete the gaps, and the horizon recedes to infinity; each line's pathologies are the other's theorems.

**The exchange closes — π/2 and 2/π are one rate, self-inverse.** The two crossings named at the head of this paper — slope → angle costs **π/2** (the atom's whole measure, $\int_0^{\infty} dx/(1+x^2) = \pi/2$, the entire unbounded ratio line totalled to a single arc), angle → slope costs **2/π** (the completed arc redistributed per unit of the observer's own ruler) — are reciprocal, and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{\pi} = 1$. That product is the content in one line: the round trip is the identity, so the two number lines are not two systems but **one closed system read two ways**, and π is not a toll paid to cross but a *self-inverse exchange rate* — spent going out, refunded coming back, nothing created and nothing lost. Exactly two constants appear, and they are π and 2: **π** the size of the closed loop ($2\pi$ the full turn, π/2 the atom's quarter of it), **2** the corner's own Jacobian ($dx/d\theta = 1+x^2 = 2$ at the hinge $x=1$, verified) — the doubling that seats the atom as a quadrant of the loop and the corner at its balance. *The real line pays π to be closed and never gets it back; the observer's line is the closure already taken, so its π is refundable — and that refund, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{\pi}=1$, is what "closed system" means.* (The earlier draft continued here into the ground-hinge question — whether the circle is *built* or *drawn*. That question is retired with the old framing: where the system came from is not considered.)

## 1.16 The root, tested by negation


The dependency map calls scale-independence the root the courts, the measure, and the projection hang from. A maintained contract should survive an attempt at demolition, so this section performs one: suppose P3 false — an external unit $u$ is available to the observer — and walk the tower, watching what falls.

**The arity forcing falls first.** With $u$ in hand, a single held quantity has scale-free content after all: $A/u$ is a contentful unary read. The floor argument of §1.2 — one quantity, no invariant, no observation — collapses, and with it the forcing of the binary atom. Arity becomes a design choice.

**The corner falls with it.** The corner's entire office (§1.1) is that balance $v = h$ is the one condition certifiable *without* external reference — the anchor that needs no ruler. Given $u$, every value is certifiable against $u$; the corner keeps its location and loses its monopoly, one calibration mark among infinitely many. The anchor is demoted to a tick.

**The swap loses its content.** The swap exchanges the two quantities' roles, and it is information-free precisely because neither role is privileged (P4 via P3: with no scale, $r$ and $1/r$ are two descriptions of one standing). Against $u$, $r$ and $1/r$ are absolutely distinguishable magnitudes; the swap becomes a substantive claim rather than a re-presentation, the two charts decouple, and the fold of §3 loses its motive — why glue what can be told apart?

**The carrier unravels.** No quotient by common rescaling means pairs live on the plane, not on the ray family: the area-to-curve collapse of §9 never happens, no $\mathbb{RP}^1$, no closure, no seam. The line stays open, and $\infty$ returns as an unreached edge instead of a held address — the crash-proof format (§3.7) loses the topology it runs on.

**The measure loses its forcing, and π its total.** The §4 derivation selects $1/(1+r^2)$ as the unique swap-invariant, unbiased weight; with the swap contentful and the closure gone, any $\sigma$-finite weight is admissible — the Cauchy becomes a choice, not a consequence. And with nothing closed there is no compact carrier, hence no total quantity of orientation, hence nothing for any amount to be a fraction *of*: the π-accounting of §10 and §12 does not miscount, it loses its denominator.

**The interleaving contrast collapses last.** With an external unit per axis available, the tensor discipline (§9.2) is no longer the grid's peculiarity but a live option: private denominators are exactly what external scales are. The sphere-versus-torus census becomes a preference.

The audit's verdict: negate P3 and the atom, the corner, the swap, the fold, the carrier, the measure, the total, and the interleaving fall in sequence — not weakened but *unmotivated*, each reverting from forced to optional. Nothing else in the premise set has this blast radius (drop P4 and the atom survives with a preferred chart; weaken P2 and composition changes while the read stands). Scale-independence is not near the root; it is the root, and this section is the felling test that certifies the map's claim rather than asserting it.

## 1.2 The atom is binary: the forcing of arity


§1.1 established two readings and the corner from scale-freedom and the one exchange the observer can perform. What it took as given is the count itself — that the observer holds *two* quantities and not three. The floor half of that count — at least two — is §1.05's ontology restated (a relative reading takes two), and carries no news. **The theorem of this section is the ceiling: no primitive operation of this observer can exceed two places.** That is an operational result, not an ontological one, and it is where the section's weight sits; floor and ceiling then meet only at two.

**The premises, named where they bear weight.** *Scale-freedom* (§1.1): no absolute reference exists, so a magnitude has no observable value except as a reading against another reading. *The carried register* (§7): the observer holds one scalar between steps, and a held value may be read against an incoming value but never composed with another held value to form a new quantity — *carry, don't compute*.

**The floor — at least two.** By scale-freedom a lone reading is not an observation: with no absolute unit, one magnitude read by itself returns nothing, and reading it against a *fixed internal* unit would be the absolute scale the observer is denied. A reading must be taken against a second reading to be a reading *of* anything. The second reading need not be an independent quantity — it may be a fixed transform of the first, as in the audio atom, where the signal is read against its own quadrature (§1.8) — but it is a distinct reading, not the bare quantity standing alone. So an observation occupies at least two slots. (This is the same fact §1.05 states from the other side: the discrete observer, holding no whole, can read only relatively, and a relative reading is one quantity against another. §1.05 places that as the ground; the argument here is one way of realizing it in a register — the *implementation* of atom-use, not a competing derivation of it. The two agree because they are the one situation named twice.)

**The ceiling — at most two.** The register carries one held value and admits one incoming value: a working set of two. A ternary atom would need a third reading present at the instant of one operation, reachable only two ways — *stored*, a second held slot, which the single scalar denies; or *manufactured* from the held values, which *carry, don't compute* forbids, since a scalar standing for the sum or ratio of two priors is exactly the composition ruled out. Both routes need what the register withholds. So an operation spans at most two slots, and any relation among three or more quantities is reached only as a *sequence* of binary atoms — which is composition (§1.3, §8), not a wider primitive.

**Arity is two.** Floor and ceiling meet. The claim is about what is atomic *for this observer*, not about whether ternary relations exist abstractly: even were one to exist, a one-scalar non-composing observer could not perform it in a single step, so it is no atom here — which is why the argument needs no proof of abstract non-existence. *And the scope runs one direction only, stated so no reviewer reads a slide the argument does not make: nothing here claims that nature, or any richer observer, is binary. Binary is a theorem about the minimal architecture (P1's single scalar, P2's carry-not-compute) and stops there. The bridge from this atom to physical generality is carried by a wholly separate argument — the cost ladder of the thesis (§7, §15.9): an $O(N)$ global pass is physically impossible at world-scale, so $O(K)$ discrete observation is the only realizable mode, which is what makes the binary atom the general primitive of scale-free observation rather than a toy. The binary claim leans on P1/P2; the generality claim leans on the cost floor; the two are never welded, and this sentence is the weld's refusal.*

**Dependency direction, stated once to kill two false loops.** A dependency audit flags two places where the prose can read as a feedback loop when the logic is one-way, and both are worth pinning explicitly. *First: binary does not depend on the corner.* Binary is forced by scale-freedom (floor) and the carried register (ceiling) alone; the corner is not a premise of it. The corner *emerges* — it is the self-certified landmark the binary atom then carries (§1.1) — so the arrow runs binary → corner, never corner → binary. Where later prose leans on "the corner" while arguing binary, that is exposition, not dependence; the proof above uses only scale-freedom and the register. *Second: the finite hold does not prove the swap.* The swap is an algebraic symmetry of the relative reading — the exchange $\tau \leftrightarrow 1/\tau$, present before any register (§1.1, §3.5) — and the finite hold merely *implements* it, choosing the representation in which the unbounded tail lands on one register (§3, and §3's own statement that unbounded storage "would not need the swap"). So the arrow runs swap → finite hold: the symmetry exists, the hold realizes it. Both corrections point the same way — the abstract structure (relative reading, its swap symmetry) is prior, and the register-level facts (binary ceiling, finite hold) are its *implementations*, not its sources. This is the architecture the whole paper now has: observer premises → relative reading and its symmetries → their register implementations → geometry → analysis, with no arrows running back up.

**Reversal comes with it.** The two slots are *held* and *incoming*. Their only distinction is temporal — which arrived first — an accident of stepping, not a structural designation of part against whole. So the pair is unordered: reading incoming against held and held against incoming are one operation under exchanged roles, not two operations. This is the exchange §1.1 used and §2 will name as the swap; here it is seen to be intrinsic to the dyad rather than an extra move laid on top. Concrete instances may pin the order from outside — audio hands the observer its reference (§1.8) — but the bare atom does not.

**Scope.** This fixes two things and no further: arity (exactly two) and the intrinsic reversal of the dyad. It does not yield the portion read, the corner, the horizon, the ratio coordinate, or the closure — those are the constructions of §1.1, §2, §3 and §8. Keeping them apart is what makes each dependency nameable.

**Where it can be pried.** Two hinges, stated rather than hidden. The ceiling rests on reading §7's bound as a *single scalar that is carried, not composed*; read instead as a finite-width store, the ceiling weakens to "bounded arity" and the dyad is no longer forced — *carry, don't compute* is the load-bearing reading. (Half-closed 2026-07-24: §1.27's carry quotient shows a wider store could hold more *readings* but never raw pairs — width changes the count of memory's units, not their scalar type — so the hinge now bears only on the count.) The floor rests on the second reading being allowed to be a transform rather than an independent quantity; drop that and the floor reads "two independent magnitudes," which the audio atom — one signal against its own quadrature — would violate, making the corpus's cleanest one-dimensional instance fail to be an atom. Both hinges are defensible on the premises already in hand; both are where a careful reader will push.

**Resize is not an atomic predicate.** The observer holds one scalar (§7) and composes by *carry, don't compute* (§1.2): a held value may be read against an *incoming* value but never against another *held* value to form a third. "Has the system been resized?" asks for a then-against-now comparison — two retained states differenced into a delta — which is exactly that forbidden composition. So *resized* is not false for the atom; it is **unaskable**: there is no second slot in which to keep the prior state, and no permission to difference two stored states were there one. Change is therefore never *within* an atom — the observer holds one scale-free read, now, with no prior to be resized from, and experiences neither growth nor shrink. "The system changes size" is a continuous observer's sentence: *change* is a difference across time, and difference needs two retained states, so it sits on the continuous observer side of §4 by the same mechanism that hides absolute size — not "the observer cannot see the system's size" but "the observer cannot difference, because differencing is a stored comparison." What change the observer *can* register, it registers across a handoff seam rather than within a hold — the construction of §6.5 — and the memorylessness that makes that the only route is not added to the atom but is §1.2's ceiling and §7's single register read together.
