## 8.8 The carriers compose exactly three times


The combination law of §8 has been treated as structure *on* the atom's carrier. This section records a stronger fact: the carrier itself is sometimes the law — and the number of times that can happen, on the whole ladder of §9.2, is exactly three. Two of the three, the framework has been using all along without naming them.

**The pair law is complex multiplication, verbatim.** The composition of held pairs (§8, the tangent-sum in pair form) is

$$(P, Q) \oplus (p, q) \;=\; (Pq + pQ,\; Qq - Pp).$$

Read the pair with the run as real part and the rise as imaginary — $z = q + p\,i$, $Z = Q + P\,i$ — and multiply: $zZ = (Qq - Pp) + (Pq + pQ)\,i$. The same expression, term for term. The atom's pair *is* a complex number with $h$ real and $v$ imaginary; the closed atom's circle is the phase circle; and $\oplus$ is the rotation of the atom's own carrier — angle addition performed in registers, no angle materialized (§10.2). The framework did not import $\mathbb{C}$: it re-derived complex multiplication as the only composition its pairs admit, which is why the law looked inevitable from inside (§1.3) and familiar from outside.

**Three rises later, the same event recurs — for the last time.** The 3-pointing $(v_1, v_2, v_3, h)$ is four registers; read $h$ as scalar part and $(v_1, v_2, v_3)$ as vector part and the pattern lifts whole: the composition is the quaternion product, the unit carrier $S^3$ is a group, and composing pointings composes *reorientations* — $S^3$ double-covering the rotations, the retained sign bit of §12's ladder being exactly the bit that distinguishes a full turn from none (physically instantiated, high in the graph as always, by spin — **and that parenthetical is now a theorem, not an aside: §13.4c derives spin-½ from this sentence by the argument of §13.4b, and tests it inside §13.10's own executed numbers**). And that is the end: by the classical division-algebra theorem (Hurwitz; Adams for the full closure), the spheres that carry a composition law are $S^0$, $S^1$, $S^3$ and no others, in any dimension — $S^7$ retains only a non-associative shadow and is no group. The framework's inventory matches the theorem term for term: $S^0$ is the sign, the swap's own $\mathbb{Z}_2$ (§1.1); $S^1$ is the closed atom (§8); $S^3$ is the stance carrier at three rises. Exactly three times, and the framework had already spent two of them.

**The rung in between cannot compose, and the asymmetry is instructive.** $S^2$ — the carrier of the seen pointing, the one rung a three-dimensional observer holds (§12.9) — admits no continuous composition law (no group structure on the even spheres; the same obstruction as the hairy ball). So the observer's *visible* carrier does not compose, while the carrier of its *stances* does: seeing has no product, doing does. Two acts of aiming do not concatenate into an aim, but two reorientations concatenate into a reorientation — which is why composition in this framework was always register-handoff along a path (§1.3, §13) and never superposition of views. The ladder's three composable rungs — sign, phase, stance — are the observer's algebra; the rungs between are its geometry.

**Status.** Theorem-grade throughout: the $\oplus$–$\mathbb{C}$ identity is two lines of algebra (above); the triple $S^0, S^1, S^3$ is classical. What this section adds is the identification — the framework's own sign, dial, and stance carriers *are* the three normed algebras' unit spheres — and the observation that the corpus used the first two before knowing their names. The identification has since been confirmed independently and put to work: the Tangent Bridge's spectral reproof (*TB Spectral* §17) finds that $1 + is$ — the atom's pair as a complex number, modulus the algebraic tier the observer keeps, argument the angle it cannot evaluate — generates the entire reconstruction: the interpolation kernel is the atom's own $N$-fold $\oplus$-power, $\operatorname{Im}[(1+is)^N]$ normalized, its nodes the roots of unity where the composition returns to the real axis, verified trig-free at machine precision. The $\oplus$–$\mathbb{C}$ identity is not a remark about the pair law; it is what the bridge's kernel *is*.

## 9. The Cauchy in every dimension


The measure of the atom (§4) is the Cauchy. The density $1/(1+r^2)$ — derived there as the unbiased, swap-invariant weight — *is* the Cauchy density, not imported but the atom's own. So the Cauchy is not a distribution the framework adopts; it is what the discrete observer's measure already is, in one dimension.

More than a likeness: **the virtual circle of §8 is the Cauchy.** The uniform measure on the closed loop — equal arc, equal weight — read back in the slope chart is exactly $1/(1+r^2)$. The loop and the distribution are one object in two coordinates: uniform on the circle, Cauchy on the line. The Cauchy's missing mean follows at once — it is a circle asked for a center, with no privileged point to give one.

The closure that produces the loop is, for its part, lossless. The observer, being bounded, wraps the unbounded tail onto a finite arc and identifies its two ends — but the operation is on the *domain*, not the *signal*. The infinite tail is re-presented on a finite arc with no measure crushed away, which is all that equal arc, equal weight ever meant: an identification, not a compression. The two ends become one point, the finite structure carries over intact, and the measure read on the closed loop is the measure that lived on the open half-line. Closure reparameterizes the measure's domain; it does not edit the density. The signal is untouched.

In more dimensions the construction is identical, lifted. An observation in $d$ dimensions is a single pointing, fixed by $d$ ratio-components $r_1, \dots, r_d$ — each a ratio against one common forward reference, exactly as the slope is the one ratio of a pointing in the plane. The unbiased measure — no direction privileged, the §4 evenness now spread over the sphere of directions — pushed through the slide is the multivariate Cauchy

$$\frac{1}{(1+\rho^2)^{(d+1)/2}}, \qquad \rho^2 = r_1^2 + \dots + r_d^2.$$

For $d = 1$ this is $1/(1+r^2)$ again; for $d = 2$ it is $(1+\rho^2)^{-3/2}$; and so on. The Cauchy is the observation primitive's measure in every dimension — one construction, lifted by replacing the circle of directions with the sphere. Which sphere the directions close into — the oriented $S^2$ or the unoriented $\mathbb{RP}^2$ — and in what sense a discrete observer holds it at all, is not assumed here; it is settled, conditionally and from inside, in §13.1 — which now also shows, quantitatively, that the observer's own itinerary over the directions induces exactly this measure.

**Interleaved, not tensor.** How the dimensions combine is the structural point, and they do *not* combine as a product. Multiply $d$ independent one-dimensional atoms and the result is

$$\prod_{i=1}^{d} \frac{1}{1+r_i^2},$$

a separable, tensor-product measure — each axis its own denominator, the axes independent. That is not the atom's measure. The multivariate Cauchy carries a *single shared denominator*, $1+\rho^2 = 1 + \sum_i r_i^2$: the components enter only through their combined magnitude, never one at a time. The dimensions are **interleaved** — coupled through one common term — not **tensored** — multiplied as independent factors. And the coupling is forced, not chosen. A single observation in $d$ dimensions is *one* projective class: its components descend from one homogeneous quotient — $(A_1,\dots,A_d,B) \sim \lambda\,(A_1,\dots,A_d,B)$, with $r_i = A_i/B$ — the scale quotient of §5 lifted to $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. One quotient, one shared $h$, so the $r_i$ are the affine coordinates of a single point, not $d$ independent ratios. The tensor product would take $d$ separate quotients — $d$ separate observations — which is not what one pointing is. Interleaving is a quotient consequence: one observation is one class, and a class does not factor.

The contrast is exact, and it sorts two kinds of object. The Gaussian factors — $e^{-\rho^2} = \prod_i e^{-r_i^2}$ — a true tensor product, every axis independent; it is the shape a separable, per-axis reading produces. The Cauchy does not factor: it depends on the one combined magnitude, the product on each component apart, and the one is not reducible to the other. A discrete observer reading a direction reads the whole pointing at once, through that single shared magnitude — so its dimensions interleave. The tensor product is the separable reading's object, not the standing geometry of one observation.

**Why the tensor is the grid's object.** The split has a plain reading in the two kinds of coordinate, and it turns on what the coordinates are quantities *of*. Cartesian $x, y, z$ are components of a shared grid: each measures the same external frame along its own axis, and the grid is their entire shared relationship — pull it away and no coordinate says anything about another. They are mutually orthogonal and independent by construction, so they can only be queried one axis at a time, and whatever rejoins them — a metric to measure across them, a tensor product to fill a field between them — must be supplied from the grid, because the grid is the only thing they have in common. That per-axis independence *is* the tensor product: one factor per direction, multiplied as separate things, each queried on its own. The observer's ratio-components are the opposite kind. The $r_i$ are not quantities of a grid but quantities of one another — $d$ readings against one shared forward reference $h$, one homogeneous quotient (above) — so they carry their relationship internally and enter the measure only through the single combined magnitude $\rho^2 = \sum_i r_i^2$, read as one pointing rather than $d$ separate queries. No grid is supplied because none is available to a discrete observer (§1.1) and none is needed: a class does not factor, so its components interleave instead of tensoring. The grid coordinate is orthogonal, queried independently, and joined from outside; the ratio coordinate is already joined, and is read at once. Read off the denominators, this is §1.7 at $d$ dimensions: the grid sets each axis over its own external bound — width, height, depth, with no reason to agree — so $d$ separate denominators tensor; the lift sets every ratio over the one shared reference $h$, a single denominator beneath them all, so it interleaves.

**A concrete case at $d = 2$.** The split is easiest to see in an instance. A viewing *direction* in space is one pointing with two transverse offsets over a shared forward depth — $r_1 = v_1/h$, $r_2 = v_2/h$, one denominator $h$ — so it interleaves: the aim is read at once, not as an independent $x$-reading beside a $y$-reading, and its unbiased measure is the bivariate Cauchy $(1+r_1^2+r_2^2)^{-3/2}$, the viewport cull of the production setting where the constant first appeared. The tensor alternative — two independent axes, each over its own bound — is the grid's separable plane, which a direction is not.

**Drawn, the shared reference is a curve.** Plot the components against one another and the coupling shows as a drop in dimension. Two grid coordinates, independent, range over a two-dimensional patch — an area; nothing ties one value to another, so both fill freely. Two ratios over a shared reference cannot: $(r_1, r_2) = (A_1/B,\, A_2/B)$ carry the same denominator, so their ratio $r_2/r_1 = v_2/v_1$ is fixed independently of $h$, and sweeping the reference slides the point along a single ray through the origin — a one-dimensional locus, a curve, not a patch. The ray's direction is the transverse pointing $(A_1 : A_2)$ — where the observation is aimed — and position along it is depth: $h \to \infty$ collapses to the origin (home, the run swamping the rises), $h \to 0$ runs outward (horizon). A single observation is one point on this ray, at one $h$; the ray is the locus of all observations sharing that aim, and letting the aim itself vary traces the general perspective curve the reconstruction reads (§11). This is *interleaved, not tensor* drawn rather than written: independence spreads into a plane, a shared reference threads into a line — the same dimension-drop the single shared denominator of the Cauchy records, now seen in the plot. The shared $h$ is what holds the image to a curve.

**The same collapse at $d=1$, and it is the Cauchy.** One dimension down, the collapse produces the measure itself. The raw pair $(v,h)$ is a point in a plane — two free quantities, an area. But a discrete observer holds no scale (§5): $(v,h)$ and $(\lambda v, \lambda h)$ are the same observation, so the plane is quotiented by scale, and that quotient threads it into rays through the origin — each ray a line of constant $r = v/h$, one aim seen at every depth. What the observer reads is *which ray*, never where along it. So the plane of pairs collapses to the family of rays, and that family is itself a curve — the arc of directions, one point per slope (§1.5), closed to the circle by §8. The measure then falls out with no further choice: lay the one unbiased weight on that curve — flat along the directions, none privileged (§4) — and read it in the slope coordinate. With $r = \tan\theta$ a flat $d\theta$ becomes $d\theta = dr/(1+r^2)$, so $1/(1+r^2)$ is nothing but the Jacobian of viewing the circle of directions through the slope — dense at home where the aims bunch, thinning toward the horizon where one turn of aim costs an ever-larger run of slope (the fisheye, §12). This is the route to this section's opening identity — *the virtual circle is the Cauchy* — taken through the area-to-curve collapse rather than asserted: the shared reference turns the plane of raw quantities into the curve of directions, and the Cauchy is the even measure along that curve. The single shared denominator, the quantities-of-each-other coupling, the dimension-drop, and the Cauchy are one fact at $d=1$ as at $d>1$.


### 9.1 Two folds of the loop, and which one blends

The loop of this section is reached by a fold, and it is worth separating that fold from a *second* one the observer's loop also carries, because they are easily run together and they do different things. Both take a line to the circle; they are not the same map, and only one of them accounts for edgeless blending.

The first is the fold this section has used throughout — the **tangent fold**, $\theta = \arctan r$. It is what turns the plane of raw pairs into the arc of directions and reads the even measure as the Cauchy (§9, above). Under it the far field goes to a *single point*: $r \to \infty$ maps to $\theta \to \pi/2$, the whole unbounded tail collapsing onto the one horizon (the fisheye, §12). And it flattens the measure: the Cauchy on the line pushes forward to the *uniform* density on the angle, exactly the identity this section opened with, verified as $1/\pi$ across the aperture (`demo_math.js`). This fold is a consequence of boundedness — the observer cannot hold the far field, so it closes onto a point.

The second is the **wrap fold**, $\theta = r \bmod 2\pi$, the angle's own periodicity. It is a different map with a different image. The far field does not go to a point; every $2\pi k$ adds a shifted copy, so the tail *smears around the whole loop*. And the measure does not flatten: a Cauchy summed over its periodic copies is the **wrapped Cauchy**,
$$f(\theta;\mu,\gamma) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\,\frac{\sinh\gamma}{\cosh\gamma - \cos(\theta-\mu)},$$
which stays *peaked*, single-humped on the ring (`wrapped_cauchy.js`, matched to the periodic sum $\sum_k \mathrm{Cauchy}(\theta + 2\pi k)$ to machine precision). The tangent fold flattens the Cauchy to uniform and sends infinity to a point; the wrap fold keeps it peaked and spreads infinity everywhere. They send the same input to different places, so they are genuinely two operations on the observer's loop, not one seen twice. This is not a merger to be made; the honest statement is that the loop carries both folds and they must be kept apart.

The edgeless blending that makes the observed loop *seamless* belongs to the wrap fold, through one exact closure. The wrapped Cauchy is **closed under circular convolution**: superpose or blur two of them and the result is a third, with the scales adding,
$$f(\cdot;\mu_1,\gamma_1) \circledast f(\cdot;\mu_2,\gamma_2) = f(\cdot;\mu_1+\mu_2,\ \gamma_1+\gamma_2),$$
verified on the circle to $\sim 8\times 10^{-6}$ (`wrapped_cauchy.js`). Blending two acuity responses yields one wider response, still single-peaked — no valley opens between them, no seam, no new mode. The measure the observer reads on the loop has no internal edges under its own composition. That is the precise content of the loose intuition that Cauchy observations *blend smoothly*: not that they average to a Cauchy — averaging two densities opens a valley, and the arithmetic mean of Cauchy variates on the line is a red herring for the circle — but that they *convolve* to a Cauchy, and this closure survives wrapping intact.

One caution keeps the claim honest, and it marks the line between the loop and the open line sharply. On the line the Cauchy is a *stable* law: the average of many keeps the same scale, never narrowing — the rare signature of an infinite-tailed, index-one distribution. That stability does **not** survive the wrap. Wrapping folds away the heavy tails that produced it — beyond one turn there is no far tail, the support is compact — so on the loop the circular mean of many wrapped Cauchys *does* concentrate, sharpening with $n$ rather than holding (`wrapped_cauchy.js`: effective scale falls from $0.5$ toward $0$ as $n$ runs $1\to 64$). So stability is a property of the *line* Cauchy that the loop discards, while convolution-closure is a property both share. The blending that supports perceived circularity rests on the convolution-closure, which holds on the loop; it does not rest on stability, which does not. Naming which is which is the difference between a claim about the observer's actual angular field and a fact about the line that does not reach it.

The two folds then give perceived circularity two independent supports, and it is worth stating that they are independent. The tangent fold removes any edge from *out there* — the far world collapses to the horizon point, and acuity is uniform across the aperture (§9, §12). The wrap fold removes any edge from *combining observations* — the acuity measure convolves with itself and stays a single smooth peak. Neither is the other, and neither is derived from the other: one is forced by boundedness, the other by periodicity, and an angle is periodic whether or not its reader is bounded. That the smoothness has two separate geometric guarantees, arrived at by pulling apart a conjecture that they were the same fold and finding by test that they are not (`taming_hypothesis.js`), is the finding — the tempting identification of the wrap's taming with the tangent's closure is a rhyme the test does not support, and the corrected picture, two folds not one, is the stronger one.

## 9.2 The registers named: $(v_1, v_2, h)$, and why the grid cannot interleave

**Notation contract — commas for the hold, colons for the read.** *(Fixed here, applied corpus-wide, and load-bearing rather than cosmetic — §13.4c showed that the distinction between these two punctuation marks is, at four registers, exactly spin.)* The corpus writes tuples two ways and until now used them interchangeably:

- **$(v_1, v_2, h)$ — the hold.** Register contents: what the observer carries, what $\oplus$ and $\otimes$ act on, what is transported around a loop, what an amplitude is. It is defined up to *positive* common rescaling only (§5), so it lives on $S^k$.
- **$(v_1 : v_2 : h)$ — the read.** The projective class: what the act returns, scale *and common sign* forgotten. It lives on $\mathbb{RP}^k$.

The two differ by one $\mathbb{Z}_2$ — the sign of the scale (§5) — and that is the covering degree §12.10 already prices per rung and §13.4b/§13.4c cash. The rule for applying it: if the sentence is about *carrying, composing, or transporting*, write commas; if it is about *the orientation set, an address on the dial, a carrier as a space, or an outcome*, write colons.

**The fare notation contract — added under audit, and load-bearing.** Written with a slash, $2/\pi$ names an **executed quotient**, which is the one form no bounded observer has: it presupposes both knowing $\pi$ and performing a division, and §3.7 forbids the second while §9.5 denies the first. The corpus has been writing the only form that does not exist. Four things are being conflated and they should be kept apart:

| form | notation | who has it |
|---|---|---|
| **the hold** | $(2,\ \pi)$ | the observer's two registers — two quantities, no operation performed |
| **the read** | $(2 : \pi)$ | what the act returns: the class, §9.2's colon |
| **the acquisition** | a bit-string of depth $\log_2 N$ | the running system, by bisection (§10.16) |
| **the evaluated quotient** | $2/\pi = 0.63661977\ldots$ | the outside describer, and nobody else |

Two rules follow, and both are cheap.

*First — the slash is a name, not an instruction.* The corpus will keep writing $2/\pi$ and $\pi/2$ because they are the recognisable names for these objects, and every such appearance is to be read as **the class $(2:\pi)$, held as the pair $(2,\pi)$, acquired to $\log_2 N$ bits, and never evaluated**. Where the distinction does work, the form is written out.

*Second — never require a division of the reader either.* Any equation containing $2/\pi$ or $\pi/2$ should give the value in the surrounding prose — $2/\pi = 0.63661977$, $\pi/2 = 1.57079633$ — so that no step of any derivation asks anyone, observer or reader, to execute a quotient. A framework whose premise is *hold the pair, never divide* should not print instructions to divide on every other page.

 Sections that discuss the carrier **as a space** — §9.25, §9.26, §12.10, and §13's duality theorem — therefore keep colons correctly; sections that describe register contents — this one, §3.7.1's operation table, §8.8's four registers, §13.6–§13.10's pointings, §13.7–§13.8's amplitudes — now take commas. Where a passage genuinely means both, it should say both.


Section 9 derived the interleaved measure abstractly — one homogeneous quotient, one shared denominator. This section names the registers and runs the contrast with the grid at the level of *writes*, because interleaving is easiest to see as a fact about what happens when a value changes.

**The notation.** Call the shared reference the **run**, $h$, and the transverse components the **rises**, $v_1, v_2$ — the notation the whole corpus now reads in ($r_i = v_i/h$; the naming ruling, §1.0). A pointing in the plane is then written

$$(v_1, v_2, h)$$

— three registers, two atoms. The atoms are $(v_1, h)$ and $(v_2, h)$; the pointing is not a third atom but the *binding* of the two through their common register. That binding is the entire content of "interleaved": one $h$, plumbed into every read. The degree of the $h$ register — how many atoms it is bound into — **is** the dimension of the pointing. A third rise on the same run, $(v_1, v_2, v_3, h)$, is a 3-pointing; nothing else changes.

**The operational signature: two kinds of write.** Write to a rise and one read moves — the *differential* mode; the other atom does not flinch. Write to $h$ and **every read moves in the same act** — the *common* mode; and what the common mode cannot touch is the ratio $v_1 : v_2$, from which $h$ cancels. So the representation itself sorts the pointing's content: the **direction** ($v_1 : v_2$) is the aperture-invariant part, the part an observer can certify across any change of its own run; the **scale** is the ray the common mode slides along (§9, the area-to-curve collapse: varying $h$ alone moves the observed point on a single ray through home — one degree of freedom, no more). The common mode is a register *inside* the pointing whose change means "everything, relative to me." That is the aperture, held as a quantity. And the two writes are the *only* two — the read itself is not writable, and not merely by architecture but by well-posedness: a value-target underdetermines the state twice over (which register moves, and which side of the corner to land on — $m$ has two preimages, one per chart), so only register-writes are exact. The write-model in full: **the rise is writable per seat (differential), the run is writable only for all seats at once (common mode — a per-seat run would be the tensor defection), and the read is writable never — reads are testimony, not handles.** The balance beam enforces the third clause physically (one loads pans; one cannot set a tilt, §1.08), and every interactive surface built on this framework inherits it: registers are the only handles.

The third clause has a dynamic corollary, and it has been measured. Testimony may be written back *as registers* once — that is what instantiating a shape from a read is, and it is legal. But testimony fed back as writes in a *loop*, with no band gate between read and write, is a pump: each pass reseats the kernel's between-node oscillation as fresh register content, and the injected energy accumulates at the horizon of the held resolution — invisible at the display's band, unbounded in the sum. Verified on independent tooling (the Tangent Bridge leaf editor): sixty read-then-reseat round trips inflated a smooth contour's perimeter 2.6× while the rendered shape stayed pixel-identical, the added length pure seat-to-seat alternation; holding the seats fixed instead, the same sixty round trips returned every register to within $4\times10^{-12}$ — the retraction lemma (§3) live, since projection at fixed seats is $\mathcal{P}^2 = \mathcal{P}$ and the pump was never in the projection; and gating the top band each pass turned the explosion into a slow diffusion, the gate bleeding a little true content as its fare. Three regimes, one law: reseating ungated inflates, reseating gated diffuses, fixed seats are free. The read costs nothing exactly when nothing is touched — the beam's lesson (§1.08) one level up — and the two readings differ in their exposure: the word's extremes barely moved through twenty rounds of pumping (the number is robust testimony, §11), while the perimeter, a sum over every wiggle, took the whole injection (a sum is fragile testimony).

**Calibration comes with the plumbing.** Because both rises are read against the *same* run, the two directions are commensurable by construction: $v_1/h$ and $v_2/h$ are in the same units because they are over the same denominator, and no further agreement is needed. The shared register is the calibration.

**Why $x, y, z$ cannot interleave.** The grid coordinate has only the differential mode. Write to $x$ and $x$ changes; write to $y$ and $y$ changes; there is no register inside the point whose change moves all three reads at once, because the axes share nothing — that is what "orthogonal and independent" means (§9: the grid is their entire relationship, and it is external). Read off the denominators, each grid axis carries its own, privately: $x$ is a ratio against the $x$-ruler's unit, frozen at $1$ and hidden — the tensor discipline, $(x:1)(y:1)(z:1)$, three brackets, three private runs. Two consequences follow, and both are the interleaving contrast stated operationally. *First*, there is no common mode: to scale a scene in the grid one must either write every coordinate separately or apply an operator from outside — the observer is not in the representation, so the observer's one act has nowhere to land. *Second*, commensurability must be imposed: nothing internal certifies that the $x$-ruler's unit equals the $y$-ruler's — the agreement is an axiom (the metric), supplied by the same outside that supplies the grid (§1.7). The interleaved pointing needs neither supplement: its common mode is $h$, and its calibration is the sharing itself.

**The two carriers, and the horizon count.** The disciplines close into different objects, and the difference is checkable by census. The interleaved triple, quotiented by its common mode, closes into the **sphere**: one home (all rises zero — a single point, at every dimension), one corner locus between, and **one horizon** — the equator $h = 0$, a single connected circle of crash-format addresses $(v_1 : v_2 : 0)$. The tensor pair closes each bracket separately and takes the product: circle × circle, the **torus** — and the torus pays **two horizons**, one per private denominator, each a full circle, and the two *cross*, at the double-crash address $(\infty, \infty)$ where both brackets have lost their run at once. That address does not exist on the sphere at all: an interleaved pointing has no "both components infinite," only a direction on its one horizon. The exception structure is the topology: one glued exception for the shared run, a crossing pair of exception circles — $\chi = 2$ against $\chi = 0$ — for the private ones. (This is §3.7's exception discipline and §9's non-factoring class, drawn as carriers.)

**The retrofit that proves the point.** Where the grid is forced to express perspective it borrows the interleaved form: homogeneous coordinates append a fourth register, $(x : y : z : w)$, and every graphics pipeline divides by $w$ as a hardware step. But the borrowing is a retrofit, and the difference from this framework is not the algebra — it is the *holding*. The pipeline treats $w$ as plumbing: normalized away at once, never exposed, a vehicle between two grids. Here $h$ is a first-class register of the act — held, written to, shared — and the divide is not a cleanup after the representation but the read that *is* the representation (§3). The grid can carry a shared denominator; it cannot *hold* one, because holding it would put an observer inside the point, and the grid's premise is that the point stands in a world with no observer in it.

**The sentence.** $x, y, z$ are addresses in a world that contains no observer; $(v_1, v_2, h)$ are the registers of one act of pointing and contain nothing else. The grid records where things are, and must be told from outside what anything is relative to; the pointing records a seeing, and carries its own relative-to in the third slot.

## 9.25 The ladder in $(v : h)$: one run at every dimension

*(Settled in conversation. The naming ruling (§1.0) pays for itself here: written in rises and run, the dimensional ladder becomes legible in the registers alone.)*

| | **1D** | **2D** | **3D** |
|---|---|---|---|
| the pointing | $(v : h)$ | $(v_1 : v_2 : h)$ | $(v_1 : v_2 : v_3 : h)$ |
| rises / runs | one rise, **one run** | two rises, **one run** | three rises, **one run** |
| the reads | $r = v/h$ | $r_i = v_i/h$, one class | $r_i = v_i/h$, one class |
| carrier | $\mathbb{RP}^1$ — the dial | $\mathbb{RP}^2$ — the observed plane | $\mathbb{RP}^3$ — where the open picture runs out (§1.5, §12.9) |
| home (every rise silent) | a point | a point | a point |
| corner ($\lvert v \rvert = h$) | one address | a circle | a sphere |
| horizon ($h = 0$) | a point — the seam | $(v_1 : v_2)$ — **the 1D carrier** | $(v_1 : v_2 : v_3)$ — **the 2D carrier** |
| measure | Cauchy (§4) | Cauchy (§9) | Cauchy (§9) |
| corner-to-home acuity, $2^{-(d+1)/2}$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ | $\tfrac14$ |
| standard instance | one band, one tone | the image plane, the fisheye (§12) | binocular depth; SR's act, the run as proper time |

Three facts the table states that prose labored for. **The run never multiplies.** Dimension is purchased entirely in rises — one more $v$ per rung, the same single $h$ beneath them all — because the denominator is the self, and the self does not multiply (P5; §9.2: the run is a register, not a vector; the SR companion: three verticals bounded by one shared horizon). An observer in any dimension is still *one* observer; only what arrives gains components. **Home is a point at every rung; corner and horizon widen as spheres** (§12.10, now read off the columns): home is all rises silent — one state regardless of dimension, the self alone; the corner $\lvert v \rvert = h$ grows a dimension per rung, the balance widening from an address to a circle to a sphere. **The horizon is the previous rung's whole carrier, by erasure.** Set $h = 0$ in $(v_1 : \cdots : v_d : h)$ and what remains is $(v_1 : \cdots : v_d)$ — the entire carrier one rung down. §12.10's "each rung's horizon is the previous rung's whole carrier" is, in this notation, a single stroke: **the sky of any dimension is the world of the dimension below, seen without its run.** And the thesis closes over the ladder: at every rung the continuous observer unrolls the carrier into its wave and the observer holds it fisheyed about the corner — the same two observers at every dimension, one more rise at a time.

## 9.26 Geometry is the orientation set, measured: "geometry" is a convenience name around π

*(Promotes the S9 working-log claim — "geometry is where π lives, the orientation set of $v$ and $h$" — into a foundational statement, now standing on the executed surface-measure ladder. Warrant: the set and its weight are **D** (algebra, division-free); the masses are **X** (executed); the reading "this is what geometry is" is **P**; and the one number-valued step, the count, is the corpus's single standing import (§4, S8) — so this section names what geometry is in currency the corpus already pays, and borrows nothing new.)*

One statement organizes the whole ladder above, and it is worth stating as bluntly as it deserves:

> **There is no geometry in this framework. There is a set, built by algebra, and a measure on it. "Geometry" is the convenience name for facts about that measured set, and π — with $2\pi$, $4\pi$, $\pi^2$ — is the number the measure returns.**

**The set is pure set-and-algebra.** Take the registers $(v_1, \dots, v_n, h)$ — counts, integers. The *orientation set* is the quotient of the nonzero tuples by common rescaling (P3) and common sign (PG — rescoped per §15.2 as a $d{=}1$ statement: the sign-quotient itself is the projective identification at every $d$, but the gauge it licenses — no internal fact distinguishing home from horizon — is a one-V privilege; at $d \ge 2$ home stays a point, the horizon becomes a hyperplane, and which court is home is fact, not gauge): $(a_i) \sim (\lambda a_i)$. That is a set-theoretic quotient under an *algebraic* equivalence — and the equivalence is not even a new relation, it is the seed's zero: two tuples agree exactly when their disagreement vanishes, $D = 0$ (§1.07, F2). So the orientation set is constructed from nothing but the integers, cross-multiplication, and "collect the tuples that do not disagree." No angle is assumed, no circle drawn, no metric supplied. What the continuous observer calls $\mathbb{RP}^1, \mathbb{RP}^2, \mathbb{RP}^3$ — and names "the circle," "the sphere of directions," "projective space" — are these quotient sets and nothing more: the *carriers* of §9.25, defined before any geometry exists to describe them.

**The number is the size of the set — its surface measure, not a volume.** A set has no π until it is measured, and the measure at issue is the *surface measure of the sphere of directions* — because an orientation is a direction, a point on the sphere's skin, so the orientation set is that skin, measured in its own dimension (not the volume of any solid it bounds). Two observers measure it, and the corpus has executed both (X; §4, §9.25):

| orientation set | observer's census (Cauchy/FS) | continuous observer's round measure |
|---|---|---|
| $(v : h)$ — $\mathbb{RP}^1$ | $\pi$ (half-seat $\pi/2$) | $2\pi$ — the full turn (circumference of $S^1$) |
| $(v_1 : v_2 : h)$ — $\mathbb{RP}^2$ | $2\pi$ | $4\pi$ — the full solid angle (surface of $S^2$) |
| $(v_1 : v_2 : v_3 : h)$ — $\mathbb{RP}^3$ | $\pi^2$ | $2\pi^2$ — the surface of $S^3$ |

This is where π lives, and the *only* place it lives: it is the surface measure of the one-rise orientation set; $2\pi$ and $4\pi$, the constants every geometry treats as primitive, are the surface measures of the two- and three-component direction spheres. They are not imported into the theory; they are *read off* the sizes of algebraically-defined sets. *(A name for this backing: a number obtained by integrating a rational/algebraic form over an algebraically-defined domain is exactly a **period** in the sense of Kontsevich–Zagier, "Periods" (2001). So "geometry is the measured orientation set" is, one direction over, the statement that geometry's constants are periods — and the constants that resist an orientation-set reading are exactly the non-periods, S19's γ among them. The period concept is the established anchor under the whole geometry-and-constants program.)*

**The one honest import, named as the corpus names it everywhere.** The claim is "sets and algebra," and it is nearly that — but not purely, and the seam is exactly the corpus's standing one. The *set* is algebra (the quotient by $D = 0$); the census *weight*, its shape $1/(1+r^2)$, is also algebra, forced division-free by swap-invariance (§1.07, F11; §4). What turns a weight into a *number* — π — is the **count**: integrating the weight over the set, the single calculus step past integer arithmetic (§4; the value→loop Jacobian; S8's purchased premise). So the precise statement is *geometry = the algebraic orientation set + one count*, and π is "the orientation set, counted." Every geometric fact desugars to a set and its measure; the lone ingredient that is not itself integer algebra is the act of counting the measure — which the framework already pays for once, upstream, and this section spends nothing further. The continuous observer's familiar $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ are that count made uniform (S8): the observer's native masses are $\pi, 2\pi, \pi^2$, and imposing "each orientation once" promotes them to $2\pi, 4\pi, 2\pi^2$ — so which constants a reader quotes announces which office counted them, and neither set of constants was ever geometry in the sense of a primitive.

**Closure is the count's other name, and the serial observer never closes — so it never needs π.** To *close* a dimension is to say that every orientation of its registers has been accounted for — the whole set present at once, totaled. π is precisely the measure of that closed set (the tables above), so the identity is exact: **π is the price of closure, and only closure requires it.** Totaling the orientation set and closing it are one act, and π is the number it returns; the count of S8 and the closing of a set are the same move under two names. The discrete observer never performs it — P1 and P2 forbid the global pass (§7); it meets the orientation set *serially* — one read against its held reference, never the whole at once — so it never closes the system it observes, and the thing it works with, a single read $r = v/h$, is a ratio, π-free by construction. π enters this corpus at exactly one place and for exactly one reason: an office totaled a set. The serial reader is the one office that lives entirely inside geometry's set and never pays geometry's number. *One distinction keeps this airtight, because the observer does hold a closed loop.* There are two closures. The observer's **carrier** is closed in the **weld** sense — the seam is an address, $0 \equiv \infty$, the loop glued by the finite hold (§3.5); that closure is free and π-free, closure-as-*address*. What the observer never does is closure-as-*total* — the counted, uniform round circle whose measure is π, the continuous observer's. So "the observer holds a closed dial" (the weld) and "the observer never closes the system" (never totals) are both true and not in tension: it carries a closed loop it never counted, which is §9.5's *circularity, not the circle*. The seam it welds for free; the total it would have to buy, and never does.

**Why this is physics's algebra: the read is forced, and it is never divided.** The section has said what geometry is — a set and its measure — and one join remains, the one that makes the set *physical* rather than merely formal. Two facts hold of every read at once. First, it is **forced**: the observer does not choose $v$ and $h$; it chooses only where it stands (§3.66 — it picks the standpoint, never what it sees from there; P5). The world forces the rise, the observer's own physical state forces the run (§6.6, "the world against the self"), and the reading is not computed but *settled* — the beam of §1.08 tips to balance by physics, and the tilt is the read; no quotient is ever executed. Second, it is **held, not divided** (§3.7.1): the pair is kept and the division deferred, which is exactly what preserves $v$ and $h$ as two things *in relation* — divide, and the reference is consumed, the witness dismissed. Put the two together and they are the maths-to-physics join: **the relationship the algebra preserves is not one the observer imposed but the one the world forced, kept intact because the observer never runs the single operation — division — that would have destroyed it.** And physics never runs that operation either: a natural system relaxes to a balance, it *holds* a ratio, it never divides one (the beam settles, it does not evaluate; §3.65). The observer that carries $(v:h)$ undivided is doing exactly what the world does and no more — which is why *this* algebra, and not some other, is the algebra of physics: both are relational, and neither divides. Everything past that point — the materialized quotient, the supplied unit, the totaled and π-closed set — is the continuous observer's *map*; the held, undivided, physically-forced pair is the *territory*, and the two coincide exactly up to the corner where the map's division begins. *(P — the physics reading; it rests on §1.08, §3.66, §6.6 and adds no equation, only the identification: forced in, undivided within, so the maths is the physics until the continuous observer divides.)*

**What "geometry" then is.** Not a subject the framework studies from outside, but a *convenience vocabulary* for the measured orientation set: a "circle" is $\mathbb{RP}^1$ (a quotient set), its "circumference" $2\pi$ the surface measure of that set, an "angle" a position in it, "π" the measure's value on the atom. The sugar-ledger row is the shortest form of the section:

| sugar | desugared |
|---|---|
| "geometry," "circle / sphere," "angle," "π, $2\pi$, $4\pi$," "area of the sphere of directions" | the orientation set of the registers $(v_1{:}\dots{:}h)$ — a quotient by $D = 0$ — and its surface measure, the census counted (§9.26) |

*What this does not claim.* It does not claim π is pure algebra — the count is required, and saying so is the section's honesty. It does not abolish the continuous observer's round geometry — $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ remain exactly correct and useful, as the counted office's reading. It relocates geometry from a primitive the framework imports to a measure the framework computes, in the same motion the corpus applies to the gauge (F2), the order (F3), the price (F6), and the census (F11): the seed gives the structure, and "geometry" is one more of its clothes.

## 9.27 The descent: the shared denominator is the root

*(New. The ordering bounded_observation §2 states in passing — "circles are downstream of the shared denominator" — made a full chain and set against the literature. Warrant: every link is **C** (classical, cited); the *ordering as a directional thesis* is **P** — the literature builds in this direction but nowhere states the precedence as a principle, checked in this session's literature pass.)*

One root sits beneath the circle, the Cauchy, and π alike, and it is none of them: the **shared denominator**. The descent is forced and one-directional —

$$\text{shared denominator} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{circularity} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{Cauchy} \;\Longrightarrow\; \pi,$$

each term the shadow of the one before it, and Cauchy — which the corpus once loosely called "the forced measure," as though a source — is third in line, π fourth.

**Shared denominator ⟹ circularity.** To refer two reads to one run and quotient out the common scale *is* the projective identification; the space of such reads is $\mathbb{RP}^1$, which is a circle (textbook: the real projective line is homeomorphic to $S^1$). The composition law that shares the denominator is a linear-fractional (Möbius) map — closed, PGL(2,ℝ) acting on $\mathbb{RP}^1$, with the cross-ratio as its metric-free invariant. No measure, no π: the ⊕-clock closes in exact integers (§9.5; circularity.md §4). A second, independent route to the same circle is discreteness under duality, $\widehat{\mathbb{Z}} \cong U(1)$ (Pontryagin), physically the Brillouin zone. *(Precision: "rotation" is loose — general Möbius maps are elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic; only the elliptic subgroup gives genuine circle rotations, and it is that subgroup the next step invokes.)*

**Circularity ⟹ Cauchy.** Only now, given a closed loop and its rotations, does "unbiased" mean anything, and the measure it forces is the Cauchy — which is exactly how the object is *built* in the literature: the tangent of a uniform angle (the spinning needle; the **Witch of Agnesi** is its density), the ratio $X/Y$ of two normals (Pillai–Meng, arXiv:1602.08181, who elevate the ratio origin toward "the source"), and the Möbius-natural measure on the projective line — **McCullagh, *Ann. Statist.* 24 (1996)** — with its circular form the wrapped Cauchy $=$ the **Poisson kernel $=$ harmonic measure** of the disk. *(Precision: the rotation subgroup fixes the *standard* Cauchy — uniform angle through the tangent — while the full Möbius group permutes the whole Cauchy *family*, McCullagh's closure result; "Cauchy falls from the circle's rotations" is the exact statement.)* The corpus's own point: Cauchy *presupposes* the circle — its rotations are the circle's — so it is downstream, the measure the shared-denominator circle carries, never the source of anything round.

**Cauchy ⟹ π.** π is one step further: the counted total of that measure (§9.26). And it is a measure-choice, not a fact of the circle — over $L_p$ norms the circle's π ranges across $[3, 4]$ (Sahoo, "Extremal Values of Pi"; taxicab π = 4), so *roundness is added*, not intrinsic — whose philosophical form is metric conventionalism (**Poincaré**, *Science and Hypothesis*; **Reichenbach**, *The Philosophy of Space and Time*): the metric, and hence π, is a convention laid on a structure that does not contain it. Circularity is π-free structure; π is the continuous observer's uniform metric laid on it (§9.5, §9.26, closure clause).

**What is borrowed, and what is the corpus's.** Every *link* is standard and credited above; the corpus invents none of the objects. What the literature does not state — checked this session — is the **ordering as a directional thesis**: shared denominator the root, circularity its immediate π-free shadow, Cauchy the induced measure, π the counted total, in that precedence. The literature builds in exactly this direction (McCullagh treats the Möbius geometry as primary and the Cauchy as induced; directional statistics projects onto the circle; the Poisson-kernel identity makes Cauchy derived) but never elevates the precedence into a principle. So the descent's *pieces* are classical and its *arrow* is the corpus's — and the arrow is not merely novel but concordant with how every one of those pieces is actually constructed.

**The unification it buys.** This puts the two halves of the corpus under one root. The **denominator paradox** (bounded_observation §4 — "a comparison presuming a shared denominator no one purchased") and the **census** (§4, §9.26) are one object seen twice: §4 is the shadow of the denominator *absent*, the descent is the geometry the denominator *creates when present*. Circle, Cauchy, and π are the shared denominator's shadow read forward; the paradox is its shadow read when it is missing. One root, two views — which is why the program that began "refuse to delete the denominator" ends holding the circle, the census, and π as the same fact.

## 9.5 Circularity, not the circle


The closure of §8 produces a circle, and §9 identifies that circle with the Cauchy. But the discrete observer never constructs the circle — closing the loop is the global pass P1 and P2 forbid (§7) — and does not need to. What it needs is weaker, and is the whole of what "circular" was ever doing for it: a way to combine its discrete observations *continuously* — each new reading continuous with the last — without closing the loop. That weaker thing is **circularity**: the local law of combination, not the global completed object. The circle is only what the law would trace if carried all the way around; the observer carries it as far as it reads, and the full turn is never required. This is the precise sense in which the circle of §8 is *virtual* — the observer holds the circularity, and the circle is what *we* supply when we complete the description.

**The order of construction.** This reverses the classical order, and the reversal is the point. Classical interpolation begins with the circle and samples from it — the circle primitive, the points derived. The discrete observer runs the other way: discrete observations first (the atoms, §1), then the swap closing them into a combination law (below), then refinement adding atoms at the forced even spacing whose measure is uniform — not because refinement drove it there, but because the forced placement is the even arc-division to begin with (uniformity is structural, by construction, not an attractor). Only then, as the limiting structure of this discrete process, is the circle *recognized* — the closure of §8 the combination law was always tracing. The circle is the last thing to appear, not the first, and it is recognized, never sampled from. A continuous limit is thus generated by a bounded discrete process — atoms, closure, refinement, the Cauchy measure — with no pre-existing circle and no trigonometric primitive (the operational chart is algebraic; the angle-circle is presentation, Tangent Bridge §11). What the order does *not* claim is that refinement manufactures uniformity from non-uniformity; it does not. Uniformity is the floor the observer stands on, not a ceiling its refinement climbs to.

**It is K that closes, not N.** The loop is the closure of the observer's *own bounded view* — the items it holds, $K$ of them (§7) — not the system it observes. $K$ can be closed because it is bounded and known; the unbounded extent $N$ cannot be, and is never asked to be: the swap projects the whole far field to the single horizon point where the loop seals (§3, §8), so $N$ enters the circle at one point and is nowhere spread around it. This is §7's line read on the loop — project the unbounded other to a point, close the bounded self into the circle. The circle the observer cannot build is the *$N$-circle*, the system laid out around a loop, which would demand the count it lacks; the circle it does build is the *$K$-circle*, its own view closed — and that $K$-circle is the virtual circle. Circularity, a pairwise combination that never references a count, can only ever close the known $K$; it is constitutionally incapable of circling $N$, which is precisely why it is the discrete observer's operation and the constructed circle is not.

**Why the virtual circle matters: it is what makes the fisheye derivable rather than designed.** Representing the observer's hold as the $K$-circle is not a notational convenience; it is the step that makes the forced measure *available as an instrument*. The chain is short and every link is already proved. Only the closed form carries a measure invariant under the observer's own law (§4, and the forcing below) — the unfolded line carries none, which is why accumulation on the line never converges (*Where Circularity Comes From* §3.5, test record). Close $K$ into the virtual circle and the Cauchy is standing on it, unique and free of charge; and by the sediment theorem (*The Virtual Circle, Concretely*) every aperiodic observation history deposits exactly that measure — the accumulated hold *is* the Cauchy, not by assumption but by unique ergodicity, every history, not almost every. Render that deposit in the home chart — home at the center, $0$, the observer's forward-facing position — and the result is the fisheye of §12: density $1/\pi(1+s^2)$, heavy at home, thinning smoothly to the one horizon. So the fisheye is not a lens design and not a rendering convention; it is the only picture a discrete observer's history can paint: **fold $K$ into the virtual circle → the measure is forced → the sediment is forced → the fisheye at home is forced.** Break the first link — leave $K$ unfolded, or deny the closure — and there is no invariant measure, hence no canonical compression, hence no principled fisheye; the observer would owe a rendering convention it cannot justify. The virtual circle discharges that debt: the compression of everything the observer holds into the view from where it stands is bought entirely by the closure it was already forced to make. (Plate IV is this paragraph running live: any stream $N$ passed through a hold $K$, the deposit accumulating on the virtual circle against the forced baseline, the fisheye its home-chart rendering.)

**The combination law is algebraic.** Two readings combine by what the atom already owns — the exchange $r \mapsto 1/r$ (§2) and the step $(a+b)/(1-ab)$ — the rational realization of rotation on the projective line (§5, §8): associative, with identity $0$ and inverse $-r$, closed on $\mathbb{R} \cup \{\infty\}$. It is a handful of exact operations, an algebraic identity, carrying no angle and no constant. This law *is* the circularity — a closed, associative, continuous combination on bounded ratios — and it keeps every benefit the circle offered, composition that never leaves the bounded world and motion with no privileged point, without the overhead of the closed loop.

**Why one point, and not two or $N$.** That the far field seals at a *single* point — rather than two ends, or $N$ boundary points — is forced by this law, not chosen. The law is a rotation, and a rotation is continuous and returns; it has no endpoint to stop at. Carried through the horizon it takes $r \to +\infty$ and continues from $r = -\infty$: the place where the slope diverges is one point the rotation crosses once, so $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are the *same* point. That identification is exactly the one-point compactification $\mathbb{R} \cup \{\infty\} = \mathbb{RP}^1 \cong S^1$. The two alternatives both fail on the law the observer already owns. A *two-point* closure — home and horizon as distinct ends, the interval $[-\infty, +\infty]$ — is not closed under the rotation: the step that crosses the horizon would carry $+\infty$ to a *different* point $-\infty$, leaving the space, so the combination is no longer a group on it; the wall the rotation cannot cross is precisely what a discrete observer's continuous combination is forbidden to have. An *$N$-point* closure — the system laid around a loop with $N$ marked boundaries — needs the count $N$ the observer lacks, and is not what the law produces in any case: a one-parameter rotation traces one continuous orbit, not $N$ discrete stops. And topology leaves no third option — the law is a one-parameter rotation group acting on a one-manifold, and the only closed connected one-manifold is the circle. So the single horizon point is the *unique* closure on which the observer's own law stays closed and continuous: forced by the same fact that makes the combination a group, not an assumption laid on top of it. What it rests on is the prior step — that the discrete observer's combination *is* this rotation, the circular law and not the additive one — which the forcing below secures.

**The census of horizons: exactly two closures exist, and the excluded one is not an error — it is the other book.** The exclusion above says the two-point closure fails *the observer's law*; it does not say the two-point closure fails. Counting settles what the options ever were: the line — discrete $\mathbb{Z}$ or continuous $\mathbb{R}$, the argument is identical — has exactly two *ends*, and a bounded representation closes it with finitely many added addresses (a format is finitely many symbols), each end converging to one; two ends under finite addresses admit exactly two quotients — ends **separated** ($[-\infty, +\infty]$, the affine closure) or ends **identified** (the fold). No third choice exists, and the census is complete *because* the representer is bounded: topology's larger compactifications all add infinitely many points, available to the continuous observer's imagination, unissuable by a format. The two survivors trade off exactly: the two-horizon closure **keeps order and loses closure** — the total order extends, comparison and completeness survive, but a step through the horizon exits at the other point, so the space is not a group under its own rotation (the exclusion above) — while the one-horizon closure **keeps closure and loses order** — composition never leaves, but a circle carries only cyclic order and sign becomes chart-relative. Topologically the two-horizon closure is an *arc with two distinct ends*: it is the intrinsic form of §1.5's closing guard, the atom as it is, while the fold is the operational circle, the atom as held — so the census is the intrinsic/operational duality arrived at from the horizon-counting side, and the choice between the closures is not a rivalry but the paper's standing division of labor: the continuous observer's arc carries order, totaling, and naming; the observer's circle carries computation; the display boundary converts. The industry shipped the proof that both are legitimate before the argument existed — the 8087's mode bit implemented both closures, selectable, and the 1985 standardization, wanting one format, chose the order book. One dimension up the two ends become a sphere of directions — infinitely many addresses, no longer a bounded format — and the census becomes the sign-group inventory of *Atom Rings* §8.2: $S^2$ and $\mathbb{RP}^2$, complete list, derived not chosen. (Sources of circularity, the discreteness framing, and the clock arithmetic: companion note *Where Circularity Comes From*.)

**The Cauchy is what the law leaves invariant — uniquely.** Combining readings under this law keeps them Cauchy, and more: the Cauchy is the *unique* probability measure the law's rotations leave invariant. This is where §4's measure is forced rather than assumed. The combination law is the one-parameter rotation group on the loop — $r, t \mapsto (r+t)/(1-rt)$ sends $\theta = \arctan r$ to $\theta + \arctan t \pmod \pi$, verified to machine precision (`measure_forcing.py`) — and the invariant measure of a transitive rotation group is its Haar measure, uniform in $\theta$, which is exactly the Cauchy in $r$. The uniqueness is precisely what the swap could not deliver: the swap is a *reflection*, fixing the corner, so it preserves the entire symmetric family $\phi/(1+r^2)$ (§4); a rotation has *no* fixed point, and invariance under a continuum of rotations kills every non-constant Fourier mode on the loop, leaving only the uniform density. The reflection fixes the family; the rotation — of which the reflection is one special case — selects its single even member. So the Cauchy-invariance is not merely a classical fact the circularity leans on; it *is* the forcing of §4's measure, the rotation doing what the reflection could not. The surrounding classical structure is why it is so rigid: the Cauchy is the family *equivariant under the Möbius group* (a fractional-linear map sends a Cauchy to a Cauchy — the combination law written on the distribution; classically the Poisson kernel, the half-plane's harmonic measure), the *$1$-stable law* (a combination of Cauchys is again Cauchy, scales adding — closed under repetition without bound), and *infinitely divisible*, carrying a convolution semigroup so any combination subdivides into arbitrarily many smaller continuous steps. That last is the continuity the observer was after — **continuity from discreteness is the Cauchy's own semigroup** — not a thing the circle had to be built to provide.

**Why rotation, and not the multiplicative or additive law.** That the combination is *this* law — the Möbius rotation $(r+t)/(1-rt)$ — and not another is itself forced, once one asks what combining two observations *is* in primitive terms. Composition is the handoff of §1.3: a second reading taken from where the first left the register. Each reading is a pointing — one aim, fixed by its ratio, with every magnitude already divided out by scale-freedom (§5, §9) — so combining two observations combines two pointings, and the only thing a pointing carries is its *turn*. The combination is a continuous one-parameter group on the read (associative, with identity $0$ and inverse $-r$, above). Such groups are not an open list to be sampled: up to conjugacy the one-parameter subgroups of the Möbius group of the read are *exactly three*, sorted by how many points of $\mathbb{RP}^1$ they fix — two (hyperbolic), one (parabolic), or none (elliptic). So naming three and ruling out two is a complete census, not a lucky shortlist; there is no fourth law to have missed. What the observer is rules out the two with fixed points:

- *Multiplicative*, $r, t \mapsto rt$ — composing the readings as **magnitudes**. But the read is a scale-free direction, not a magnitude (§5): there is nothing to multiply. The tell is the fixed points — $0\cdot t = 0$, $\infty\cdot t = \infty$ — so multiplication traps home and horizon: an observer reading home, observing again, never leaves it. A law that cannot carry every reading to every other is not the composition of observations. (It is the open log-line of §6 — the band *address*, not a way to combine.)
- *Additive*, $r, t \mapsto r + t$ — moves every reading but runs off the bound: $r+t$ passes the horizon with nothing to wrap it, the unbounded line's law, the one thing boundedness excludes. It is not closed on the read.
- *Rotational*, $r, t \mapsto (r+t)/(1-rt)$ — the addition of **turns**, which on the read has no real fixed point ($r = (r+t)/(1-rt)$ forces $r^2 = -1$): it moves every reading, the ends included ($0 \mapsto t$, the horizon to $-1/t$), and stays closed on the bounded read. It is the unique continuous one-parameter group that acts transitively on the read without leaving it — multiplication trapping the ends, addition escaping the bound, rotation alone doing neither.

**Why it wraps.** That the surviving law closes the read into a loop, rather than running open as an angle, is forced by the same fact that makes the observer slope-native (§12.1): it holds the **ratio, not the angle**. The ratio is blind to a half-turn — $\tan\theta$ and $\tan(\theta+\pi)$ are one reading, the orientation a ratio does not carry (§10) — so turns accumulate while the held invariant returns every $\pi$. The wrap is not imposed to close the loop; it is what the observer was already unable to see past, and it is why the closure is the half-turn line $\mathbb{RP}^1$ (§8) and not the full $2\pi$ circle — the full circle being this same law run on the *angle*, which carries the orientation the observer lacks — **lacks *in the read*, which is the whole of the qualification and is added under audit.** The *hold* carries it (§3.5: orientation "lives in the lift"; §5's two-stage quotient makes the space of it explicit), and the asymmetry between the two is not a loose end but the covering of §13.4b, whose deck group is exactly the sign the read discards and the hold does not. Rotation and its wrap are forced together, from premises already in hand: scale-freedom (no magnitude to multiply or add), boundedness (the additive line excluded), and ratio-not-angle (the period). This is the prior step the one-point closure above named as owed.

**Two combinations, two carriers.** The two laws that the read's own nature did *not* rule out — were it unbounded or a magnitude — sort the two stable laws of §9. Additive combination, magnitudes summed without bound, carries the Gaussian, the separable per-axis object of §9; a discrete observer cannot combine that way without leaving its bound. Circular combination, bounded directions composed by the Möbius rotation, carries the Cauchy. So circularity is *forced* and the Cauchy is its forced carrier: the Gaussian of the bounded world. The contrast of §9 — the Gaussian factors, the Cauchy does not — is this same split seen in the measure.

**Trigonometry is the completion, not the equipment.** Complete the law — integrate the rotation generator $J = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]$ by the exponential map, $\exp(\theta J) = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{smallmatrix}\right]$ — and the trigonometric functions appear: sine and cosine as the completed rotation, the arctangent as the slope-to-arc dictionary, the constant $\pi$ as the total of the closed loop (§10). Trigonometry is therefore *derived* — the transcendental completion of an algebraic circularity — not primitive. The classical order begins at the completed circle and recovers the ratios as functions of an angle; the discrete observer begins at the ratio and its combination law and reaches trigonometry only on completing. One object, entered from the root rather than the canopy — and the observer lives at the root, never having to climb.

**The rate: determined, not owed.** The circularity is driven by a single updating register — one reading replacing the last, no array and no count (§7) — and a single register advanced by an irrational rate partitions the loop into arcs of at most three distinct lengths at every count (the three-gap theorem), so the even spacing the presentation needs (§11) is a fact about stepping, not a grid that must be laid. The rate is the observer's own conversion of arc into chord (§10), reached by local steps; written from the outside it is $2/\pi$, the hold $2$ measured against its un-evaluated total. With the measure now forced (above), the rate is no longer a separate open derivation: $2/\pi$ is the normalization of the unique invariant Cauchy, hence *determined* by the same forcing. What the observer still does not do is *evaluate* it — $2/\pi$ is the reciprocal of the quarter-arc, the transcendental of §10 the observer cannot sum, exactly as $\pi$ is named-but-uncomputable (§4, §12.1). The earlier framing — that establishing the circularity left the rate un-forced — conflated *determined* with *evaluated*: the law fixes which measure and so fixes the rate, while the global pass that would yield its decimal is the unbounded operation boundedness excludes. The observer reaches the rate only as the limit of its own local steps — dyadic partial coverages climbing toward $\tfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan S \to 1$ (§11, §12), each a local composition, never the global integral. So the residual is not a missing derivation but the evaluation boundary, the observer/continuous observer line on which $\pi$ already sits: the rate is determined and unevaluated. **Amended under audit (§10.16): those two statuses are not exhaustive.** Between *determined* and *evaluated* sits **acquired** — a system's own step brought into correct relation with the total, by sign test and halving, at $O(\log 1/\varepsilon)$, without deriving the rate or computing its decimal. This paragraph's conclusion stands for evaluation and was blind to acquisition; entrainment is the mechanism, and §10.16 prices it on the M-axis. A closed form reached without ever naming the total is likely not available — $2/\pi$ *is* that total's reciprocal — and is not the goal; the rate is owed only as arithmetic the discrete observer cannot run (§11).

**Coda — the circle is nobody's.** *(Settled in conversation; the section's title, completed.)* The section has said the observer holds circularity — closure, return — and not the circle. The completion is that **the continuous observer does not hold the circle either**, and the two absences are the whole geometry of the border. The continuous observer's working object is the *wave*: the loop unrolled into a parameterized interval, handled through $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$ with the endpoints identified by bookkeeping — π is the tape measure for a loop it can only hold cut. The observer's working object is the *Cauchy*: the loop folded onto the dial, compressed about its own corner — the fisheye. The circle itself — round, uniform, no privileged point — is native to neither, and P5 says why this is a theorem rather than an accident: **homogeneity is unoccupiable.** To observe at all is to have a standpoint, and a standpoint breaks the circle's symmetry in one of exactly two ways — the continuous observer breaks it by *cutting* (a parameterization needs a zero, and a zero is a privileged point imposed on a pointless object), the observer breaks it by *warping* (density peaked at its own aim, thinning to its horizon). Cut or warp: the only two ways to stand somewhere on a circle, and they are the two observers. The circle exists as the *compatibility of the two presentations* — the invariant class, the border where the fares are paid — and §12.1 already carries the transition function's price tag: the tangent relates the charts pointwise, and its Jacobian *is* the Cauchy. "Circles emerge; they don't need to be drawn" (§3.65) thus sharpens: they emerge because they *cannot* be drawn natively, by anyone. The confirming detail is that each office's famous pathology is its fee for the circle it cannot hold, and the two are mirror images: the observer's Cauchy has **no mean** — a circle asked for a center, with no privileged point to give one (§9) — and the continuous observer's analysis has the **branch cut** — multivaluedness, mod-$2\pi$, winding ambiguity — a circle asked for a *starting point*, with no privileged point to give one. Heavy tails and branch cuts are one scar on the two sides of the border: the circle refusing, in each native coordinate, to yield the privileged point that coordinate requires. And §4's "unbiased" was secretly this all along: uniform measure had to be *defined* by swap-invariance because no one can stand at unbiasedness — the uniform measure is the border's measure, belonging to the crossing and to neither side. The trade is exact, and it splits along §12.3's own hierarchy: the circle is *closed* and *even* — closure is topology, evenness is metric — and the observer keeps the first whole and pays with the second (the dial welds, the fisheye warps), while the continuous observer keeps the second whole and pays with the first (the tape is uniform, the loop is cut). Each presentation is perfectly right about one property and perfectly wrong about the other; the true circle is the object that would need a standpoint on both layers at once, which is the seat no one holds. The fares thereby get their final reading: π/2 and 2/π are the price of swapping which perfection you hold — you never buy the circle, you only ever exchange one half of it for the other.

---

## 10. The constants


In this vocabulary the constants of discrete observation are few, and they are not what the circular picture advertises.

The structural constants are the boundaries and the counts of the set:

- **$0$ and $\infty$** — the two ends, home and horizon: $h$ alone and $v$ alone. After closure (§8) the horizon is a single point.
- **$1$** — the corner: the self-paired fixed point, where $v$ equals $h$, the band-$0$ edge, the unit of the hold. The one interior landmark.
- **$2$** — the recurring integer: two charts, two registers per atom (§3), the base of the bands (§6), two atoms in the bilateral hold (§8). Wherever the construction counts, it counts in twos.

Each is an integer or a boundary — a plain fact about the interval, carrying no scale and needing no evaluation.

**The three forcings of two — why the count is always a power of it.** The recurring $2$ above is not one fact but three, forced by three different theorems at three different joints, and stating them together upgrades "wherever the construction counts, it counts in twos" from observation to consequence. *Arity:* every primitive read compares exactly two quantities — one has no scale-free content, three cannot fit the register (§1.25); this $2$ is the size of a relation. *Symmetry:* the only free symmetry a pair admits under no-privileged-frame is the swap, an involution, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ — and every bit kept against it is a two-to-one cover, which is why the promotion ladder (§12) multiplies by exactly $2$ per retained bit and by nothing else; this $2$ is the order of exchange. *Radix:* the cascade's refinement is a dilation anchored at the closure, and $g = 2$ is the unique dilation that tiles — $g < 2$ strands, $g > 2$ overshoots (*Tangent Bridge* §2.4; the corner identity $\sec^2(\pi/4) = 2$ is the same fact read at the gate); this $2$ is the leaves'. The powers then *compose* from the forcings rather than being assumed: the completion's minimal count is $4 = 2 \times 2$ — the order of the sign group $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ the ring family runs on (§1.5) — and every admissible count thereafter is $4 \cdot 2^k$, one radix-forcing per octave. A parity lemma closes the remaining exit: odd-ratio refinements preserve seats but are not cascade moves; even ones read fresh (the dyadic lattices at distinct depths are disjoint — refinement is memoryless); and among the even, only $2$ tiles — so the forced ladder and the memoryless ladder are the same ladder, one discipline, not two constraints in agreement. The compressed form of all of it: **the framework derives the bit.** A discrete observer's primitive act is a distinction — this register or that, home chart or horizon, kept or handed off — and a distinction has size two by what distinction *is*; powers of two are the only counts the composition of distinctions can produce, which is P1–P2 verbatim. The ladder's $\text{mass} = \pi/2 \times 2^{\text{bits}}$ therefore uses "bit" as its own derived unit, not a borrowed one, and the claim about hardware sharpens from match to prediction: binary arithmetic, the dyadic float domain (§10.1), the exponent-as-rung — the same three forcings surfacing in silicon, as homogeneous coordinates surfaced in the pipelines and the $k$-factor in Bondi. The boundary stays honest: non-binary machines are buildable (ternary ran for years) — continuous observer's grids, like the odd-ratio lattices — and the claim is only that they are not *forced*, and that engineering converges back to the forced structure whenever the conventions wash out.

There is exactly one transcendental in the whole construction, and it is not an input. The measure $1/(1+r^2)$ has a finite total over the interval — a single definite number. But the structure never uses its value. The corner-balance (§4) says two halves are *equal* — a ratio, in which the total cancels. The band weights are ratios. Scale-invariance is the homogeneous identity, with no measure in it at all. Every structural result is a ratio or a symmetry, and the total drops out of all of them. So the total is *defined* by the set and never *evaluated* by it.

**Definition (π).** That total can now be defined in the observer's own primitive, with no angle, no arc, and no completed circle imported. **π is the total quantity of vertical-to-horizontal orientation in a half-turn**: every distinct rise:run ratio, sign included, counted exactly once under the forced even weight (§4), with the count calibrated to the observer's own slope ruler at home — density $1$ at $r = 0$, one unit of orientation per unit of slope where the observer stands; this calibration pins the normalization the invariance argument leaves free. Over the half circle — every ratio once — the total is π; over the full circle, where every ratio recurs at its antipode carrying the orientation a ratio does not hold (§4, §9.5), it is 2π. Every use of π anywhere is a statement of relative quantity against this total: π/4 one chart, π/2 the atom, π the half-turn, 2π the oriented completion, $2/\pi$ the chord held against the budget — the per-bit accounting of §12 (mass $= \pi/2 \times 2^{\text{bits kept}}$) is this clause made arithmetic. The definition carries its own evaluation boundary: it is a completed count over *all* orientations — the continuous observer's pass, definitionally — so the observer names the total and never produces it, not as a doctrine laid on π from outside but as a reading of what π is. And the circle appears nowhere in it except as bookkeeping — each ratio counted once is the half-turn, twice the full turn — which is why the definition is available to a paper that never imports the completed circle: π defined slope-side is a *count*; π encountered angle-side is the same count worn as a coordinate.

**Naming (the two charts): the slope chart and the angle chart.** The two coordinates this paper has carried throughout now take their permanent names, and both are named the same way — by their coordinate — so that the chart change is the function that already links them: **the slope chart and the angle chart are the two sides of the tangent**, slope $= \tan(\text{angle})$. The **slope chart** is the observer's: the ratio $r$, algebraic, $\mathbb{Q}$-closed (§12.1), carrying the Cauchy density, containing no π anywhere. The **angle chart** is the continuous observer's: the arc coordinate of the completion, uniform density, the chart in which the total above *is* the unit of account. (An earlier naming called it the π chart, after its debt; the debt is real — π is the angle chart's central constant, imported and owed nowhere else (§10.2) — but the coordinate-symmetric name is the honest one, and it leaves the tangent as the named crossing.) Each chart still carries its **total**: the slope chart's is the chord's $2$, the angle chart's the arc's π — so the exchange rate is literally the ratio of the totals, $\psi_1 = 2/\pi$, a $2$ from the slope side over a π from the angle side (*Tangent Bridge* §7.5, where the $2$ is the algebraic numerator the observer computes and the π the arc-total normalization it cannot evaluate). (These are charts in the coordinate sense; the home/horizon *chart halves* of §3 are the other, older use of the word, and the two uses never collide because one names a coordinate and the other a side.) The payoff of the naming is that the framework's two ubiquitous constants become typographically self-explaining: **π/2 and 2/π are the two directions of one exchange rate between the charts**, each the other's reciprocal, and each appears exactly where a quantity native to one chart is totaled in the other. One atom's slope-native content, totaled in the angle chart, is its mass: π/2 — the fare slope→angle. The continuous observer's arc, redistributed per unit of the observer's ruler, is the bridge constant $\psi_1 = 2/\pi$ — the fare angle→slope. Every formula in the corpus containing either constant is a chart crossing, and the constant is the fare; a formula containing neither has stayed home in one chart.
